course.title: English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric
course.description: Take sentences apart and rebuild them, test arguments, scan Shakespeare and read Austen the way a critic does.
course.audience: A fluent adult reader who wants to write with precision and read literature critically. No grammar course or literary training is assumed; school terms are defined when they appear.

paragraphs: You already speak English all day, and this course asks you to look at it the way a maker looks at a tool. Writers study how sentences are built because a well-built sentence can be checked: you can find who acts, you can see where the verb sits, and you can spot the words that do nothing. Critics study speeches, poems and stories for a similar reason. Once you can name the parts, you can say why a line moves you or why a paragraph falls flat.

The course has twelve lessons in four parts. The sentence takes sentences apart into clauses, joins them with the right marks and puts actors back where readers expect them. Argument and rhetoric looks at how an argument is built and how famous speakers persuaded. Reading poetry covers metre, sound and the sonnet. Reading prose and drama looks at point of view, irony and the shape of a plot.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, so you meet a question only once you have been shown what it needs. School terms are explained where they first appear.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the verb and its subject in a line of verse, even when the words are shuffled.
You'll be able to join two clauses with the mark that says what you mean.
You'll be able to rewrite a passive or padded sentence so that the actor leads and every word counts.
You'll be able to split an argument into claim, grounds and warrant, and say where it can be attacked.
You'll be able to scan a line of pentameter and say who is telling a story and how far to trust them.
introduction.prerequisites: You should read English comfortably; no grammar or literary training is assumed.

concepts.title: Inside a clause
concepts.summary: Find the finite verb and its subject, tell an object from a complement, and separate independent clauses from dependent ones.

concepts.title: Joining two clauses
concepts.summary: Repair a comma splice and choose between a semicolon, a colon, a dash and a conjunction by what each mark says about the relation.

concepts.title: Actors and actions
concepts.summary: Move actors into subjects and actions into verbs. Switch between active and passive, unbury nominalisations and count the words a revision saves.

concepts.title: Claim, grounds and warrant
concepts.summary: Take an argument apart with Toulmin's model: the claim and the grounds offered for it, the warrant that links them, the qualifiers and rebuttals that limit it.

concepts.title: Ethos, pathos, logos and kairos
concepts.summary: Trace the four appeals through Douglass's Fourth of July oration and Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, and see how each speech uses its moment.

concepts.title: Figures of repetition and balance
concepts.summary: Recognise anaphora, antithesis, chiasmus and tricolon in Dickens, Lincoln, Douglass and Shakespeare. Say what each figure does to an argument.

concepts.title: Metre and scansion
concepts.summary: Count syllables and place the beats of iambic pentameter. Hear a feminine ending, and tell a rising iamb from a falling trochee.

concepts.title: Sound and image
concepts.summary: Hear alliteration and assonance. Tell a metaphor from a simile and name the tenor and vehicle of a figure.

concepts.title: The sonnet and its turn

concepts.title: Who sees and who speaks

concepts.title: Structure: arcs and turning scenes
concepts.summary: Map a play onto Freytag's pyramid, find its climax, and count the scenes that turn a value from hope to loss or back.

steps.headline: The word that changes with time

lead.text: The exercise in the opening works because English marks time on a single word. Take “She opens the window” and move it into the past: “She opened the window.” The word “opens” changed and nothing else did. Go the other way, into the present, and the same word is the only one that has to move.

A verb that changes like this is called a finite verb. “Finite” means limited: the verb is tied to a particular time, and often to a particular person too, as in “I open” and “she opens”. Every complete statement has one at its centre. Without one you have only a label, such as “the window”. Nothing has been said about what happens.

afterFigure.text: That gives you a test that works on any sentence, no matter how oddly it is arranged. Put the sentence into a different time and watch which word has to change. Forms such as “to open” or “opening” never change with time, so they are not finite verbs, a difference we will need again before the end.

lead.text: Try the test on the sentence from the opening.
Sonnet 18 does not put its words in the order we would use in conversation, so position will not help. The tense test still works on any word order.

reveal.text: You applied the tense test. “Declines” would become “declined”, so it is the finite verb. Ask who or what declines and you get “every fair”, which the next screen names.

lead.text: Finding the verb is half the job. A verb needs someone or something to carry out the action, and asking who or what does it gives you the second half. Take “She opened the window”. Ask who opened, and the answer is “she”. That word is the subject.

The subject and its finite verb are enough to say something complete: “She opened” tells you that someone did something at a particular time. A group of words built on a subject and its finite verb is a clause. Everything else in a sentence hangs on a clause, adding detail about when, where, how or why. Those added words and phrases are modifiers.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets Shakespeare's line beside a plain one. The words are shuffled, yet the same two anchors appear, “declines” and “every fair”, with the modifiers hanging off them. In ordinary prose the line would say that every beautiful thing at some time falls away from its beauty. Next comes what can follow the verb.

lead.text: Some clauses stop after the verb, as in “The dog barked”. Others carry on, and what comes next depends on the verb. Some verbs pass their action to something. In “The wind rattled the shutters”, the shutters are what get rattled. A word or phrase that receives the action of the verb is an object.

Other verbs, such as “was” and “seems”, pass nothing on. They link the subject to a description. In “The wind was cold”, nothing is done to the cold. The word tells you what the wind is like, and a word that does that after a linking verb is a complement.

afterFigure.text: To tell them apart, ask what the word after the verb does. If it receives the action, it is an object. If it says what the subject is or is like, it is a complement. Either can be longer than one word. The subject of “The tall oak by the gate fell” is built round one noun, “oak”. The other words describe it. The noun at the centre of a phrase like this is its head noun. An object can even be a whole clause: in “She remembered what he had said”, the clause “what he had said” is what she remembered.

steps.headline: Is the last part of “The storm shook the roof” and of “The storm was fierce” an object or a complement?

lead.text: Two clauses share a subject and end differently. The test from the last screen settles each one.

workedSteps.text: Find the verb and subject in each: “the storm shook” and “the storm was”.
“Shook” acts on something: “the roof” receives the action, so it is an object.
“Was” only links the subject to what follows: “fierce” says what the storm is like, so it is a complement.

steps.headline: Find the head noun of the object in “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”.

lead.text: Sonnet 18 gives the next sentence to work on. Find its object, then reduce the object to its head.

reveal.text: You stripped the phrase back to its core. Every object is a phrase built round one noun, and the other words describe it.

workedSteps.text: Find the verb and its subject: “do shake” and “rough winds”.
Ask what the winds shake: “the darling buds of May”. That whole phrase is the object.
Take away the describing words and keep the one noun they describe.

lead.text: So far every clause could stand as a sentence on its own. “The dog barked” could, and so could “She opened the window”. A clause like that is independent. Some clauses have a subject and a finite verb and still cannot stand alone.

Add one small word at the front and a clause starts to lean. “We stayed inside” is complete. “Because it was raining” has a subject, “it”, and a finite verb, “was raining”, yet it leaves you waiting to hear what followed from the rain. A word such as “because”, “when”, “if” or “which” that makes a clause lean on another is a subordinator, and a clause it opens is a dependent clause.

afterFigure.text: A dependent clause lets a writer attach a reason or a condition to the main statement, and a long sentence can stack several. What it never does is stand alone. Take away the clause it leans on and the sentence is left hanging.

lead.text: Sonnet 130, line 3 holds two clauses side by side. Only one of them could be a sentence on its own.

reveal.text: The little word at the front decided it. Independent clauses make sense alone; dependent ones wait for the rest.

steps.headline: One finite verb for each clause

lead.text: Every clause is built on one finite verb, so counting the finite verbs counts the clauses. It is a quick way to see how a long sentence is put together. In “Anna decided to leave when she saw the rain”, the finite verbs are “decided” and “saw”. That makes two clauses: “Anna decided to leave” and “when she saw the rain”.

Take care with verb forms that carry no tense. “To leave” is an infinitive, the plain form of a verb, usually with “to” in front. A participle is a form such as “walking” that adds detail without fixing a time. In “Walking home, Mia hummed a tune”, “walking” is a participle and “hummed” is the only finite verb. Neither infinitives nor participles change with time the way a finite verb does, so neither counts.

afterFigure.text: Counting this way is the fastest check on a long poetic sentence. Verse often runs one sentence across several lines, with clauses folded inside clauses, and the finite verbs show where each one is anchored.

lead.text: Apply the count to two lines of Sonnet 116.

reveal.text: You counted one verb for each clause. In long poetic sentences, that is the fastest way to see how the thought is built.

blocks.text: Say “The dog chases the ball” out loud. Now tell the same story as something that happened yesterday. Go through the sentence word by word and notice how many of the five you had to alter.

One word is doing a job the others cannot do. It fixes the sentence to a moment in time, and the rest of the sentence hangs from it. Poets rely on this. They shuffle words into odd orders to fit a rhythm or a rhyme, and a reader who knows where to look can still find the thread.

Take a line of Shakespeare: “And every fair from fair sometime declines.” It reads strangely, with two words that look the same and no obvious place to begin. This lesson shows you where to begin, and how far the same method takes you through a few lines of verse.

recap.keyIdea: Find the finite verb first, then its subject. What follows is an object or a complement, and a clause opening with “if” or “when” cannot stand alone.

blocks.text: You began with the one word that moves when a sentence changes time, and used it to pick out “declines” in a line Shakespeare had shuffled. Next you asked who does it and told an object from a complement. After that you decided which clauses can stand alone, and you finished by counting three finite verbs in two lines of Sonnet 116.

lessons.title: Joining two clauses

lead.text: Two complete statements side by side raise a small problem, because the writer must decide what goes between them. Each is an independent clause, in the last lesson's words, so each could stand as a sentence. “The shop closed” is one and “We went home” is another.

The plainest choice is a full stop: “The shop closed. We went home.” The reader gets two sentences and works out the connection alone. To make one sentence, the writer needs a joiner. The usual one is a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction, a short word that links clauses of equal weight, such as “and”, “but”, “so”, “or” and “yet”. Each names a relation. “And” adds. “But” sets one against the other. “So” gives a result.

afterFigure.text: A comma on its own is too light for the job. “The shop closed, we went home” runs two complete statements together with nothing but a comma between them. Editors call this a comma splice, and in formal writing it counts as an error. Some writers splice on purpose. Frederick Douglass told a Fourth of July audience in Rochester in 1852, “You may rejoice, I must mourn”. The abruptness makes the two fates collide.

lead.text: Back to the message in the opening.
Here is a sentence with only a comma between its halves.

reveal.text: You named the fault. A writer who splices deliberately, as Douglass does, is breaking the rule with a purpose. A writer who splices by accident is simply making an error.

lead.text: A semicolon offers a second way to join two complete statements. It does the joining by itself, so no conjunction is needed: “The hall emptied; the street filled.” The mark tells the reader that the two statements are one thought, and the reader supplies the connection. It suits a link that is clear without a word to spell it out.

Both sides of a semicolon must be able to stand as sentences. “The hall emptied; because the lights went out” fails, since the words after the mark cannot stand alone. The semicolon follows the same rule as the full stop, with a whole clause on each side.

afterFigure.text: The second case shows what a semicolon makes possible. In “Alice chose tea; Ben, coffee; Carol, juice” the second and third clauses have no verb. The reader borrows “chose” from the first clause, and a comma marks the gap where the verb was left out. Because commas are already busy inside each clause, the semicolons keep the clauses apart.

steps.headline: Repair “The rain stopped, the match began” in two ways.

lead.text: Two of the fixes from the last screens, applied to one splice.

workedSteps.text: Check each side. “The rain stopped” and “the match began” are both full clauses, so a comma alone cannot join them.
Option one: swap the comma for a semicolon. “The rain stopped; the match began.”
Option two: keep the comma and add a conjunction that fits. “The rain stopped, so the match began.”

steps.headline: Find the verb Douglass leaves out of his second and third clauses.

lead.text: Douglass joins three charges with semicolons. The second and third are shorter than the first.

reveal.text: The comma marks where the verb was dropped. Commas inside each clause are already busy, so the semicolons separate the clauses.

workedSteps.text: Read the first clause whole: “To him, your celebration is a sham;”
The second clause has a subject, “your boasted liberty”, and a complement, “an unholy license”, but no verb.
Which verb from the first clause is understood here?

steps.headline: A mark that promises an explanation

lead.text: The colon works differently from the semicolon. It follows a complete statement and makes a promise: what comes next will explain or spell out what you have just read. “The reason was simple: the bridge was closed.” The first part could stand alone, and the second part says what the simple reason was.

Shakespeare uses a colon this way at the end of line 2 of Sonnet 18. He tells the beloved that they are more lovely and more temperate, and the lines that follow set out why summer falls short. The test is the same as for the semicolon. The words before a colon must be able to stand as a sentence.

afterFigure.text: A colon fits when the second part answers the question that the first part raises. When the second part only adds another fact, a semicolon or a conjunction suits better.

lead.text: Three sentences use a colon. Test the words before each one.

reveal.text: You tested the words before each colon. Only a complete clause can make the promise that the second part keeps.

lead.text: You now have several ways to join the same pair of clauses, and each says something different. A comma with a conjunction names the relation. A semicolon says the clauses are one thought and leaves the relation to the reader. A colon says the second clause explains the first.

A dash is the sharpest of these. It breaks the sentence and makes the reader stop. Lincoln's Bliss copy of the Gettysburg Address uses dashes to hold “we can not dedicate” apart from “we can not consecrate”, so that each verb lands harder than the one before.

afterFigure.text: Choose by asking what you want the reader to know. A conjunction suits a relation that matters, a semicolon suits two statements that simply belong together, and a colon suits a second statement that explains the first.

lead.text: One sentence can use several of these marks, and the count from the last lesson still works. Find each subject with its finite verb, then ask whether that clause could stand alone. “The ferry was cancelled; the crowd waited: the next boat was due at noon” has three independent clauses, one before each mark and one at the end.

A dependent clause does not add to the count of independent clauses. In “The ferry was cancelled because the wind rose; the crowd waited”, the clause opened by “because” leans on the first clause, so the sentence has two independent clauses and one dependent clause.

afterFigure.text: The marks do not change the count. A semicolon, a colon or a conjunction sits between complete clauses, and each complete clause with its own finite verb is one more to count.

blocks.text: You are texting a friend about last night. You waited at the stop and the bus never came, and you want to say so in one sentence. You type “We waited, the bus never came” and press send. The message reads perfectly well.

Put the same words in an essay and an editor will circle the comma. The words are identical, so the trouble lies in what a comma can carry. The marks between two statements do real work. A full stop, a comma, a semicolon and a colon each tell the reader something different about how the statements fit together, and a writer who chooses well says more than one who chooses by habit.
This lesson takes plain statements and tries each mark between them in turn. You will see which joins hold and which fail, and what the good ones say.

lessons.title: Actors and actions

steps.headline: Who did it, and where the sentence says so

lead.text: Almost every sentence about an event has an actor, the person or thing that did it, and a receiver, the person or thing it was done to. In “The dog ate the sandwich”, the dog is the actor and the sandwich is the receiver. English lets you tell the story from either end. “The sandwich was eaten by the dog” describes the same event with the receiver in front.

The first version is in the active voice, which means the subject does the action. The second is in the passive voice, where the subject receives it. The passive is built from a form of “be” and a past participle, here “was eaten”, and the actor moves into a phrase that begins with “by” or drops out of the sentence.

afterFigure.text: Notice what else changed. The passive sentence is two words longer, and it opens with the sandwich, which the reader meets before knowing why it matters. The active sentence puts the doer first and gets on with the story.

lead.text: Back to the smashed window. Tell the first answer the other way round.

The passive does something else that is easy to miss. The actor sits in an optional “by” phrase, so it can be left out without a trace. “The sandwich was eaten” is a complete sentence, and it does not say by whom. That helps when nobody knows who acted, or when the actor does not matter. It also lets a writer avoid naming someone, which is why you meet sentences such as “The decision was taken to close the office.”

So ask of any passive sentence who did this, and whether the reader should know. If the actor matters, bring it forward into the subject. The active version usually saves words as well, because the passive needs a form of “be” and often a “by”, and those add two words that the actor's name does not need.

afterFigure.text: The passive is not wrong. It earns its place when the receiver is the point of the sentence. The skill is knowing which sentences are hiding someone.

steps.headline: Make “The report was written by the analyst” active.

lead.text: Three moves turn a passive into an active sentence.

workedSteps.text: Find the actor. The “by” phrase names the analyst.
Make the actor the subject: “The analyst”.
Turn “was written” into a plain past verb and keep the receiver as its object: “The analyst wrote the report.”

steps.headline: Make “Mistakes were made by the finance office” active.

lead.text: The passive can delete the actor altogether. That is honest when nobody knows who acted, and evasive when the writer does.

reveal.text: The actor was in the sentence all along, hidden behind “by”. Ask of every passive: who did this, and should the reader know?

workedSteps.text: The receiver is “mistakes”, and the verb is “were made”.
The actor is named inside the “by” phrase.
Move the actor to the front. Which words become the subject?

lead.text: Rewrite the sentence, then count what your version needs.

reveal.text: You moved the actor to the front and dropped “was” and “by”. The passive's extra words disappeared, and the sentence now opens with whoever acted.

steps.headline: A noun that hides a verb

lead.text: The passive is one way for a sentence to lose its energy. A second way is to take an action and turn it into a noun. “Approve” is a verb: “The board approved the plan.” Turn it into the noun “approval” and the sentence needs another verb to carry it: “The board gave approval to the plan.” The action is still there, but it sits inside a noun while “gave” does almost nothing.
A noun made from a verb in this way is a nominalisation. Common endings are -tion, -ment, -al and -ance, as in “announcement”, “arrival”, “performance” and “agreement”.

afterFigure.text: The repair is to turn the noun back into a verb. “The board gave approval to the plan” has seven words and “The board approved the plan” has five. Look for a weak verb such as “gave”, “made”, “took” or “conducted” holding up a noun that is really an action. Remove both and the action takes over the sentence.

lead.text: This sentence buries two verbs. Count the words before and after.

reveal.text: You turned two noun phrases back into verbs. Fewer words, and the committee now does something.

lead.text: A sentence can lose force in a third way, through padding. Some words add nothing a reader would miss. A frame such as “it is a fact that” only announces that a claim is coming, and the claim could simply arrive. Some modifiers repeat what the noun already says, as in “a free gift”, since a gift is free already. Phrases such as “at this point in time” take five words to say “now”.

Cutting these is the easiest edit to count. Read the sentence, mark the words you could remove without changing what it claims, and subtract. If the claim survives the cut, the words were padding. If something went missing, put it back.

afterFigure.text: Padding often goes with the other two faults. A writer who is unsure of the claim reaches for a frame, and a writer who avoids naming the actor reaches for a long phrase. Cutting padding is often the first step towards seeing who is acting.

lead.text: Here is one sentence through the edits. “The delivery of the parcels was completed by the courier on Monday” has twelve words. Put the courier first and you get “The courier completed the delivery of the parcels on Monday”, which has ten. Unbury the verb inside “delivery” and you get “The courier delivered the parcels on Monday”, which has seven.

Five words went, and nothing the reader needed went with them. Each edit gave something back as well. The first restored a name, and the second restored a verb that moves. Put the actor first and the action in the verb, then cut whatever carries nothing.

afterFigure.text: The order of the edits does not matter much. What matters is that you ask of a sentence who acts and where the action is, and then which words could go.

blocks.text: A shop owner arrives to find the front window smashed and asks the staff what happened. One of them says, “The window was broken by Sam.” Another says, “The window got broken.” Both describe the same event in nearly the same words, yet the owner learns something different from each. The first answer names a person. The second leaves a gap where the person should be.

Where a name sits in a sentence, and whether it appears at all, is something a writer controls. Put the person who acts first and the sentence moves. Bury the action inside a noun and it sags. Business reports, official letters and school essays are full of sentences that do the second, and most can be repaired in seconds once you know what to look for.
We start with the smashed window and then work through longer sentences, counting the words each repair saves.

lessons.title: Claim, grounds and warrant

steps.headline: What an argument is made of

lead.text: An argument is an attempt to get someone to accept a conclusion by giving them a reason. Take a coach choosing a team: “Pick Mia, because she scored twenty goals this season.” Two things are on the table. The conclusion the coach wants accepted, “Pick Mia”, is the claim. The fact offered to support it, that she scored twenty goals, is the grounds.

To find the claim in any passage, ask which statement the others are reasons for. To find the grounds, ask what the speaker points to as evidence, which is usually a fact you could check or something observed. The claim can come first or last. Words such as “because”, “since” and “so” often sit between the two and show which way the reasoning runs.

afterFigure.text: Grounds alone do not make an argument. Twenty goals says nothing about picking Mia until a further idea is added, and that idea is the next stop.

statements.text: Pick Mia for the team.
Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Every light in the house is on.
Someone is at home.

lead.text: Three statements about a bridge. Ask which one the other two are reasons for.

reveal.text: You looked for the conclusion. The claim is the statement the others are reasons for: here, closing the bridge.

statements.text: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.
The museum should open late every Thursday.
Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.
The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.

steps.headline: The rule that links the two

lead.text: Look again at the coach's argument. Twenty goals is a fact about Mia, and “Pick Mia” is an instruction. A fact cannot give an instruction by itself. Something else carries you from one to the other, and it is a general belief the coach holds: players who score a lot help a team. Nobody says it aloud, because it seems too obvious to need saying.

That belief is the warrant, the general rule that licenses the step from grounds to claim. The word comes from the same root as a search warrant, a document that gives someone the right to act. Grounds are particular and the warrant is general, and the warrant is usually left unstated.

afterFigure.text: Because the warrant is hidden, it is where arguments are often weakest. An opponent might reply that goals scored against weak teams prove little. Nobody can make that reply until the rule has been written out.

lead.text: Back to your friend and her dog. Separate what she said from what she assumed.

steps.headline: Label the parts of: “Rain is forecast, so take a coat, since forecasts are usually right.”

lead.text: Use the three questions from the last screens.

workedSteps.text: Find the conclusion. “Take a coat” is what the writer wants accepted, so it is the claim.
Find the fact offered for it. “Rain is forecast” is a particular fact, so it is the grounds.
Ask what rule links the two. “Forecasts are usually right” is general, so it is the warrant.

steps.headline: Label the rule behind: “His fingerprints were on the knife, so he handled it.”

lead.text: The claim and the grounds are given. The rule between them is the part left out.

reveal.text: Writing the rule out shows what the argument assumes. Once it is written, a lawyer can ask whether prints show handling at the relevant time.

workedSteps.text: The claim is “he handled the knife”.
The grounds are “his fingerprints were on the knife”.
Name the unstated rule that links the two.

statements.text: The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
It is Saturday lunchtime.
The café will be busy.
Cafés are busy at Saturday lunchtime.

lead.text: Once a warrant is written out you can test it. In the knife argument nobody disputes the fingerprints, because they were found and photographed. A defence lawyer attacks the rule instead. Prints show that someone touched the knife at some time, but the argument needs them to show that the defendant held it during the crime. The grounds are untouched, and the argument is weaker all the same.

That is why it pays to name the warrant when you read an argument. Disagreeing with the grounds means arguing about facts. Disagreeing with the warrant means arguing about what the facts prove, and that is where most real arguments are won or lost. A careful speaker knows this, and builds some defences into the argument in advance.

afterFigure.text: The next screen shows two of those defences, which are small additions that change how far an argument claims to reach.

lead.text: A careful speaker admits the limits of a claim before an opponent can point them out, and there are two ways to do it. A qualifier says how strongly the claim is made, with words such as “in most cases”, “very likely” or “presumably”. A rebuttal names the conditions under which the claim would fail, and it often opens with “unless”.

Take “The ferry will in most cases sail on time, unless fog closes the harbour.” The qualifier is “in most cases” and the rebuttal is “unless fog closes the harbour”. Neither weakens the argument. Both make it harder to knock down, because the exceptions an opponent would raise have already been granted. An argument with no qualifier claims to hold every time, and a single exception then breaks it.

afterFigure.text: Qualifiers and rebuttals are the speaker's honesty built into the argument. They say how sure the speaker is and what would change that.

statements.text: The harbour has been clear all week.
In most cases,
The ferry will sail on time.
Unless fog closes the harbour.
Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Very likely,
Mia will help the team.
Unless an injury keeps her out.

lead.text: One sentence holds both a qualifier and a rebuttal. Read for the word that measures how sure the writer is.

reveal.text: You separated the two. A qualifier and a rebuttal concede in advance the exceptions an opponent would raise, so the claim is harder to knock down.

statements.text: Harriet leads every poll by eight points.
Probably.
Harriet will win the election.
Unless rain keeps her supporters at home.
The air pressure is falling fast.
Very likely.
It will rain tomorrow.
Unless the front stalls over the coast.

lead.text: There is one more part. A warrant is a rule, and a rule can itself be doubted. A speaker who expects doubt supplies backing, which is support for the warrant itself. Backing differs from grounds. Grounds support the claim, and backing supports the rule that links the grounds to it.

A doctor argues that a patient should take an antibiotic because the infection is bacterial. The warrant is that antibiotics treat bacterial infections. The backing is the clinical trials behind that rule, which nobody needs to cite until someone doubts the rule.

afterFigure.text: A full argument can have six parts, and you will rarely meet all of them in one passage. The skill is to notice which are present and which are missing.

statements.text: The infection is bacterial.
Almost certainly,
The patient should take an antibiotic.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections.
Clinical trials show that antibiotics clear bacterial infections.
Unless the patient is allergic.
The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
Forensic studies show that ridge patterns are individual and transfer by contact.

lead.text: Label each statement by the job it does. A particular observation is grounds, a general rule linking it to the conclusion is the warrant, and an “unless” clause is a rebuttal.

reveal.text: Sorting by job shows the shape: a fact, a general rule, a conclusion and an exception. Only one statement is a general rule.

statements.text: Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise.
Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.
The price should return to its old level.
Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen.
The council should plant trees on Gale Street.
Gale Street is hotter in summer than streets that have trees.
Shade lowers the temperature of a street.
Unless the roots would damage the pipes below.

lessons.orientation: Take an argument apart with Toulmin's model: the claim and the grounds offered for it, the warrant that links them, the qualifiers and rebuttals that limit it.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Your friend leans across the table and says, “Get a dog: mine makes me so happy.” She means it kindly, and it sounds like a reason. You nod, and then you find yourself hesitating, though you could not yet say what is bothering you.

Most persuasion has this shape. There is a piece of advice, a fact offered to back it, and a connection that nobody mentions because it seems obvious. When the connection is sound you never notice it. When it is shaky you feel the shakiness without knowing where it comes from.

In 1958 the philosopher Stephen Toulmin offered a way to find it. This lesson takes his method and uses it on small cases: a bridge inspection, a fingerprint on a knife, a museum's opening hours. You will learn to name the parts of an argument and to see where it can be attacked.

intro.promise: By the end you'll split an argument into claim, grounds and warrant, and spot the qualifiers and rebuttals that limit it.

recap.keyIdea: Every argument has a claim, grounds and a warrant that links them. Qualifiers and rebuttals limit it, and backing supports the warrant.

blocks.text: You picked the claim in a bridge argument and counted what your friend had said aloud and what she had left unsaid. You named the warrant behind a fingerprint case, found the qualifier in an election forecast and numbered the warrant in a pricing argument.

recap.nextHook: Structure is only part of persuasion, and the next lesson begins with three people who each have one sentence to win your trust as you choose a guide for a mountain trip.

lessons.title: Ethos, pathos, logos and kairos

lead.text: Aristotle noticed that a speaker persuades through three channels at once, and he called them proofs. The first is ethos, the speaker's character and credibility. A listener trusts a mechanic who says “I have fixed engines for thirty years” before hearing anything else she says.

The second is pathos, the feeling a speech arouses in the people hearing it. “Picture your own child waiting at the school gate in the dark” works on pity and fear, and it does so with an image and no argument. The third is logos, the argument carried by the words themselves. “Three of the last five buses ran late and the timetable has not changed, so it will run late again” reasons from a fact to a consequence.

afterFigure.text: Real speeches mix all three, often inside one sentence. Reading well means asking of each part what it is working on: the speaker's standing, the listeners' feelings or the chain of reasoning. The name of the appeal follows from the answer.

model.source: An invented meeting of bus users

spans.text: I have ridden the number 9 to work for thirty years.
Picture your own child waiting at the school gate in the dark.
Three of the last five buses ran late and the timetable has not changed, so it will run late again.
Our coaches have trained county champions since 1998.
Picture a child swimming her first length, grinning at the far wall.
Pupils who join at six reach county standard by twelve, so starting early pays off.

lead.text: Ask whether the sentence reasons or moves, and who it speaks for.

On 5 July 1852, the day after Independence Day, Frederick Douglass stood up in Rochester, New York, to speak to an audience that had gathered to mark the nation's independence. Douglass had escaped from slavery as a young man and was by then a well-known speaker and writer. The people in the hall expected praise of the founders and of the republic.

A speaker in that position has an unusual problem. He must be heard as someone entitled to speak on the subject, and he is addressing people who see the day very differently from him. Whatever else his speech does, it has to settle first whose voice the audience is listening to.

afterFigure.text: His opening moves answer that problem. He sets himself apart from the audience's celebration and says so plainly, and the rest of the speech then rests on what that position allows him to say.

lead.text: Here are the first lines of the speech. Ask what gives Douglass the right to say them.

reveal.text: His standing as someone who lived what he describes is his proof. A speaker who builds trust in this way is relying on ethos.

spans.text: I am not included within the pale of this glorious anniversary!
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.
You may rejoice, I must mourn.
As chair of this society for twelve years, I have signed every one of its accounts.

steps.headline: Name the appeals in: “As a lifelong farmer, I ask you to picture the empty field next spring.”

lead.text: One sentence can carry two appeals. Separate them by what each part works on.

workedSteps.text: Split the sentence by what each part works on.
“As a lifelong farmer” says who is speaking and why to trust her. That is ethos.
“Picture the empty field” asks you to feel a loss. That is pathos.

steps.headline: Name the appeal in Douglass's contrast between two outcomes of one sunlight.

lead.text: Douglass sets one sunlight against two outcomes. “Stripes” are the marks of the whip, placed beside the audience's own “life and healing”.

reveal.text: The contrast is physical, so the feeling is hard to avoid. The image is chosen to move the listeners, which is the work of pathos.

workedSteps.text: The audience hears two images side by side: one warm, one cruel.
The image is chosen to move the listeners. It offers no step of reasoning.
Name the appeal that works through the audience's feelings.

spans.text: The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.

lead.text: Eleven years later, Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a cemetery on the Gettysburg battlefield. The battle had been fought in the first days of July, and in November the war was still going on. The main speaker that day was Edward Everett, who talked for about two hours. Lincoln followed with a speech that lasted around two minutes.

Lincoln opens with a date. “Four score and seven years ago” is an old-fashioned way of naming a number of years. A score is twenty. The phrase asks his listeners to count back from the day they stand in to the moment the nation began, and what he says about that moment is the base on which the rest of the speech is built.

afterFigure.text: A speaker who starts by pointing to the start of the nation gives the audience something to measure the present against. Working out where the phrase leads is the next task.

lead.text: Lincoln gave his speech in 1863. Count back through the years his opening phrase names.

reveal.text: The year belongs to the Declaration of Independence, so Lincoln rests the nation on its founding premise rather than on the Constitution. From that premise he argues what the war tests, which is logos.

spans.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation,
conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
Now we are engaged in a great civil war,
testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.

steps.headline: From a premise to a test

lead.text: Now the date can do its work. Lincoln points to the founding year and attaches a premise to it: the new nation was dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal. The sentences that follow draw out what that premise implies, one step at a time, until he reaches the duty that falls on the people listening. That chain of reasoning is the logos of the speech.

Lincoln builds trust as well. He says “We have come to dedicate a portion of that field”, and the “we” makes the president one of the mourners. And he moves the audience with a plain phrase for the soldiers' sacrifice: “the last full measure of devotion”.

afterFigure.text: All three appeals are present in a few lines. Which one leads depends on the sentence, and a short speech can still use each of them.

steps.headline: The right words at the right moment

lead.text: Every speech is given somewhere, on some day, to people in a particular mood. The Greeks had a word for the right moment, kairos, which means an opportune time. Kairos is the fit between an argument and the occasion on which it is made. The same words can fall flat on one day and land on another.

A speaker can use the occasion in two ways. One is to make the occasion itself the subject, so that the audience's reason for being in the room becomes part of the argument. A coach three goals down at half time can say that this is exactly where the team has always found its best football. The other is to use the place as evidence, as when a speaker standing in a rebuilt school says that this is where the old building burned down. In both cases the argument would be weaker anywhere else.

afterFigure.text: Kairos is the hardest of the four to see, because it is not in the words alone. To find it, ask what the speech would lose if it were read on a different day in a different place.

model.source: An invented speech at a library opening

spans.text: We are standing where the old school burned down.
Tonight it is a reading room, and that says what this town values.
We are three goals down at half time, and that is exactly when this team has always found its best football.

lead.text: Douglass, invited to speak at a celebration of independence, asks his audience: “What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?”

reveal.text: He made the holiday's own meaning the argument. Lincoln did the same with the ground: “We are met on a great battle-field of that war” uses the place itself as evidence.

spans.text: What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?
I answer, a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
We are met on a great battle-field of that war.

lessons.orientation: Trace the four appeals through Douglass's Fourth of July oration and Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, and see how each speech uses its moment.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: You are choosing a guide for a mountain trip, and each of three candidates gets one sentence to win you over. Before any of them has described a route or a price, you have already leaned towards one. You could not say exactly why, but the sentence told you something.

Speakers have long known that persuasion works through several channels at once. Some of it comes from who is speaking. Some comes from what the speaker makes you feel. Some comes from the reasoning, and some from the timing, since the same words can fall flat on one day and land on another. More than two thousand years ago Aristotle gave names to the first three, and later teachers added a fourth.
We will use those names to take apart two famous speeches, one by Frederick Douglass in 1852 and one by Abraham Lincoln in 1863.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the appeal in a line of a speech and say how Douglass and Lincoln use their moment.

recap.keyIdea: Ethos, pathos and logos persuade through the speaker, the feelings and the argument. Kairos is how well a speech fits its moment.

blocks.text: You found the standing behind Douglass's “yours, not mine” and the image of “stripes and death” behind his contrast. You dated Lincoln's opening to 1776, and you saw why a holiday and a battlefield each suited the speech given there.

recap.nextHook: A speech persuades through its words as well as its reasoning, and the next lesson begins with Caesar's report of a victory, which people still remember as three short parts.

lessons.title: Figures of repetition and balance

lead.text: Start with the simplest way to build a sentence the ear can hold. Say a few words, then say the same few words again at the start of the next part, and again at the start of the part after that. In June 1940 Winston Churchill told the House of Commons what Britain would do if the country were invaded, and every promise began the same way: “we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills.”

afterFigure.text: The opening words “we shall fight” come back each time, so they act as a frame, a shape that does not change. Only the place changes. The listener stops waiting for the grammar and takes in the places one by one, and the promise grows with every repeat. Repeating the opening of successive clauses is called anaphora, from a Greek word meaning “carrying back”.

The device works in prose as well as in speeches. When a passage keeps starting the same way, ask what is staying still and what is moving. Dickens does it in one of the best-known openings in English fiction, and that is where we go next.

spans.text: in the fields and in the streets,
pluck up that which is planted

lead.text: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities with one sentence that keeps a single frame going for ten clauses. Here is its start. Count how often the frame opens a clause.

reveal.text: Four times in this extract. Look at what Dickens puts inside the frame: best against worst, wisdom against foolishness. Setting ideas against each other like that is the next device.

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening
Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

lead.text: In Dickens's sentence the frame stays still while something else moves: best against worst, wisdom against foolishness. Putting two opposed ideas side by side like this has its own name, antithesis, from a Greek word meaning “setting against”. What makes it work is that the two halves are built the same way.

Neil Armstrong's words as he stepped on to the Moon show it plainly: “one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind”. Both halves have the same shape, a number, an adjective, a noun and “for”, so the eye runs along the first half and then finds each word's opposite in the same place in the second. Small meets giant, and one man meets all of mankind.

afterFigure.text: The matching shape does the lining up. Without it the contrast would be a loose remark, and with it the reader feels the opposition before working it out. Antithesis and anaphora often turn up together, as in Dickens, where “it was” repeats while the opposed ideas sit in the same slots. To spot an antithesis, look for two halves of the same shape and check whether their key words oppose each other.

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

steps.headline: Name the figure in Lincoln's “what we say here” against “what they did here”.

lead.text: Lincoln tells his audience that the world will “little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here”. Set the two halves side by side.

reveal.text: The matching frame makes the opposition collide, so the speech enacts its own modesty: words matter less than deeds.

workedSteps.text: Put the two halves side by side: “what we say here” and “what they did here”.
The grammar is identical. Only the words change: “we” against “they”, saying against doing.
Name the figure that balances opposed ideas in parallel form.

spans.text: The world will little note, nor long remember

lead.text: Antithesis keeps the order of the words and swaps the ideas. A third device keeps the words and swaps their order. In 1961 John F. Kennedy told Americans: “Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country.” Read the key words in each half. The first half has country and then you, and the second has you and then country.

Write the pairs as letters and the pattern shows. Country is A and you is B, so the first half runs A B and the second runs B A. Draw lines between the matching words and the lines cross, like the Greek letter chi, which looks like an X. That is why the figure is called chiasmus. When the very same words come back, as they do here, the figure has a narrower name, antimetabole.

afterFigure.text: A reversal makes a sentence feel finished, as if it had folded back on itself, and it lets a speaker turn a claim round to show its other side. That is why it often marks a turning point. The proverb says you can take the boy out of the country but not the country out of the boy, and the same swap holds it together. Read the key words of the first half in order, then read the second half, and see whether they come back the other way round.

lead.text: Frederick Douglass puts this sentence at the turning point of his Narrative, just before he fights back against the man who has been beating him. Look at the order of the terms in each half.

reveal.text: The terms come back reversed: man, slave, then slave, man. The reversal suits a passage where Douglass stops being treated as property. Because the same words return, the stricter name is antimetabole.

lead.text: There is one more shape, and it is the oldest. People like to count off three. “Ready, steady, go” and “lights, camera, action” both take three beats and stop. A series of three parallel parts is called a tricolon, from the Greek for “three limbs”. The parts share a shape and are usually close in length. The series sounds complete at three, because two feels unfinished and four starts to sound like a list.

Thomas Jefferson's phrase in the Declaration of Independence is a tricolon of rights: “Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness”. The third part is the longest, and it is the one that lands hardest. Speakers use that habit on purpose, putting their strongest idea last so that the series builds as it goes.

afterFigure.text: A tricolon can be made of single words, short phrases or whole clauses. What matters is the parallel shape. It can also carry another figure inside it. When three parts start with the same words, the tricolon and the anaphora work at the same moment, and the next screens show how those layers add up.

lead.text: Lincoln ends the Gettysburg Address with a promise that “government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth”. Look at how the parts are built.

reveal.text: Three parallel members make a tricolon, here three phrases that share one noun and differ by one word. Lincoln's lines a little earlier use the same device, and they use more than one at once.

spans.text: shall not perish from the earth.

lead.text: Real sentences seldom use one device alone. A few lines before the “of the people” sentence, Lincoln says that “in a larger sense, we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate, we can not hallow this ground.” The words “we can not” open each part, so the line has anaphora. There are three parts, so it is also a tricolon.

The verbs add a third layer. To dedicate is to set something aside by a formal act. To consecrate is to make it sacred in a ceremony, and to hallow is to make it holy. Each part is weightier than the one before, so the series climbs. Lincoln is saying that the soldiers have already done more to this ground than any speech could.

afterFigure.text: In practice, reading figures means naming each device you can find and then asking what they do together. Here the repeated frame tells the crowd that a list is under way, and the climb tells them it is heading somewhere. The devices from the earlier screens do not compete. They sit in the same sentence. Check a line for a repeated opening, for opposites in matching halves, for words that come back reversed and for a series of three, because one line can pass more than one of those checks.

spans.text: in the fields and in the streets,

lead.text: Back to where we started. In English, Caesar's report of his victory reads “I came, I saw, I conquered”. Read it the way you now can, and look at how each part begins.

reveal.text: All three parts begin with “I”, and there are three of them: anaphora and a tricolon in a single short line, which is why it is so easy to remember.

lessons.orientation: Recognise anaphora, antithesis, chiasmus and tricolon in Dickens, Lincoln, Douglass and Shakespeare. Say what each figure does to an argument.

blocks.text: In 47 BC Julius Caesar is reported to have summed up a victory in what is now Turkey in three words of Latin. In English we usually give them as “I came, I saw, I conquered”. More than two thousand years later people who never studied Latin still quote the line, and most of them can say it without a slip.

Plenty of short sentences about big events are forgotten within a week. This one lasted because of the way it is built. Its parts have the same shape and fall into a rhythm, so the ear learns the pattern after one hearing and does much of the remembering for you.

This lesson takes that pattern apart. You will meet four ways of shaping a sentence so that it holds in the memory and pushes an argument along, with famous lines from Churchill, Dickens, Kennedy and Lincoln to show each one at work. Writers have names for them, and you will use those names by the end.

lessons.title: Metre and scansion

lead.text: Clap along to a nursery rhyme and you will find that your hands do not land on every word. They land on some sounds and skip others. To see which, break each word into its syllables, the chunks you say with one push of breath. Hickory has three syllables, hick, o and ry. Dickory has three as well. Dock has one.

Say “hickory dickory dock” aloud and you tap only three times, although you have said seven syllables. Some syllables are louder and longer than the rest. We call those the stressed syllables, and the others are unstressed. The stressed ones are the beats that your hands find.

afterFigure.text: Two counts are now in play, and the rest of the lesson depends on keeping them apart. Syllables are everything you say. Beats are the stressed ones among them. A poet who wants the ear to settle chooses words so that the beats come at regular spacing, and that regular pattern of strong and weak syllables is what we call metre. The next step is to look at the patterns poets use most.

lead.text: Say the first line of the rhyme at an even pace. Your hands will want to tap on the stressed syllables and skip the rest.

Many nursery rhymes start on a beat: HICK-o-ry, HUMP-ty. Much of English poetry does the reverse. It starts with a light syllable that leans into a heavy one, the way you say “hello”, with the weight on the last syllable. A pair of syllables with the weak one first and the strong one second is called an iamb. “To-DAY” and “be-LONG” are each one iamb, with the capitals marking the beat.

An iamb is a foot, which is the name for one repeating unit of a line. Poets name a line by its foot and by how many feet it holds. Five iambs in a row make ten syllables with a beat on every second one. The Greek for five is penta, and a metre is a measure, so this line is iambic pentameter. Shakespeare used it for most of his plays and for his sonnets, and its rhythm sits close to the way people speak English, which is part of why it is easy to listen to.

afterFigure.text: The figure marks the stressed syllables in two such lines. Read each one aloud and lean on the marked syllables. You should find the pattern pulling you along, a light syllable and then a heavy one, five times over.

lead.text: Say the first line of Sonnet 18 slowly, and tap once for each vowel sound. Do not count words; count syllables.

reveal.text: Ten, with the beats on I, pare, to, sum and day. That is five iambs, so the line is iambic pentameter.

lead.text: With the pattern in hand you can mark up any line. The marking is called scansion. You write out the syllables and decide which are strong, then you compare them with the pattern. In a regular line of iambic pentameter the beats fall on the even-numbered syllables, the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth. The odd-numbered ones are the weak syllables between them.

Speech and pattern do not always agree. In the first line of Sonnet 18, “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?”, the word “to” is light in everyday speech and you would hurry past it. The pattern puts it in a beat position. The best reading sits between the two. “To” gets a little more weight than usual, and the line moves in time.

To scan a line, count its syllables first. Then mark which ones are strong and compare them with the pattern. The next screen does this for a line by Milton, and the one after asks you to carry on alone.

steps.headline: Scan “They also serve who only stand and waite”.

lead.text: This is the last line of Milton's sonnet on losing his sight. Follow each move in turn.

workedSteps.text: Count the syllables: they, al, so, serve, who, on, ly, stand, and, waite. Ten.
Mark weak and strong in turn, starting weak: they AL so SERVE who ON ly STAND and WAITE.
The five beats sit on every second syllable, so the line is iambic pentameter.

lead.text: This is the third line of Sonnet 18. The first two beats are placed for you, and you carry on from there.

reveal.text: You stepped through the line two syllables at a time. The rhythm is regular, and the light words sit between the heavy ones.

The first beat is on “winds” and the second on “shake”.
Keep going in steps of two syllables.

lead.text: Every line so far has had exactly ten syllables and ended on a beat. Shakespeare's lines sometimes run over. In Macbeth, when he hears that his wife has died, he says “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow”, which is eleven syllables. Marked for the beat it reads to-MOR-row AND to-MOR-row AND to-MOR-row, with all five beats on even-numbered syllables and a weak eleventh syllable left over at the end.

afterFigure.text: The extra syllable does not change the metre. The line still has five beats, so it is still iambic pentameter. That is why a line is named by its beats. Count the feet first, then check whether a spare syllable hangs off the end.

lead.text: Sonnet 116 describes love as a fixed mark that looks on storms without being shaken. Line 6 is below. Count carefully, tapping once for each vowel sound.

reveal.text: Eleven: “-ken” trails after the last beat on “sha-”, so the line has a feminine ending and is still pentameter.

steps.headline: Falling feet and the names of lines

lead.text: Every foot so far has risen, weak then strong. Turn it round so that the strong syllable comes first and you get a trochee. Most nursery rhymes are built from trochees because they start on a beat: TWIN-kle TWIN-kle LIT-tle STAR. The last foot has lost its weak syllable, which is common in rhymes. When you clapped along earlier you were counting trochees.

The foot and the number of feet together name a line. Two names to learn: a line of three feet is a trimeter and a line of four is a tetrameter. Five feet give the pentameter you already know. Four iambs make iambic tetrameter, which has eight syllables. Four trochees make trochaic tetrameter. Length changes the feel. A longer line has room to think, and shorter ones feel brisk, closer to song.

afterFigure.text: Set the two lines side by side and the difference is clear. One rises towards each beat and the other falls away from it. Two lines can hold similar numbers of beats and still feel quite different, depending on which way their feet face.

lead.text: Use what you know about the names of lines. A foot of this kind has two syllables.

Shakespeare's witches in Macbeth chant to a different beat from his human characters. Say their line aloud, DOU-ble, DOU-ble, TOIL and TROU-ble, and notice which syllable of each foot carries the beat.

reveal.text: The witches chant in trochaic tetrameter. Each foot falls, and the last weak syllable is dropped. Shakespeare gives his supernatural speakers a metre unlike his humans' iambic speech.

blocks.text: Think of a nursery rhyme you learned before you could read. Without deciding to, you probably said it with a steady pulse, and if you were sitting down your hand may have tapped along. The words did not ask for that. Something in the way they were chosen and ordered made the pulse hard to avoid.

Verse has always worked like this. Before a poem says anything, it sets up a beat, and the ear settles into it the way it settles into the ticking of a clock. Shakespeare's sonnets, Dickinson's hymn-like stanzas and a rhyme for toddlers all lean on the same machinery, a pattern of strong and weak sounds repeated line after line.

This lesson starts with a nursery rhyme and ends with a line of Shakespeare. On the way you learn to count the sounds in a line, find where its beats fall and name the pattern. You need only your ears and a finger to tap with.

recap.keyIdea: Metre is a pattern of weak and strong syllables. Iambic pentameter has five rising feet, ten syllables and beats on the even ones.

lessons.title: Sound and image

lead.text: Take a tongue-twister apart and the cause is easy to hear. In “Betty Botter bought some butter, but she said the butter's bitter”, nearly every important word opens with the same b sound, and your mouth has to keep restarting it. Repeating a consonant sound at the start of nearby words is called alliteration.

Poets use the same effect gently. A cluster of s sounds can hush a line, a cluster of hard k and t sounds can make it snap, and m sounds can make it hum and slow down. What counts is the sound and not the spelling. “Knee” and “nose” alliterate, because both begin with an n sound, even though the first is spelled with a k. “Cat” and “city” do not, because one begins with a k sound and the other with an s.

afterFigure.text: Keats opens “To Autumn” with “Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness”. The m sounds in mists and mellow make the line slow and warm, like the season it describes. When you read poetry, say a line aloud and listen to how the nearby words begin.

lead.text: Here is a twister built on a single sound. Say it aloud, and listen to how each word begins.

reveal.text: Six. The same sound opening nearby words is what the ear picks up as a pattern. Poets use it with more restraint, as the next line shows.

lead.text: Sonnet 30 opens: “When to the sessions of sweet silent thought”. Say it aloud and listen to how each word begins.

reveal.text: Three words share the opening sound: sessions, sweet and silent. The hushed s suits a line about silent thought.

lead.text: Consonants are one half of a word's sound. The other half is the vowel, the open sound at the centre of a syllable, such as the a of “cat” or the oo of “moon”. A vowel can echo too. When stressed syllables near each other share a vowel sound, whatever consonants surround it, the effect is called assonance.

Edgar Allan Poe's “Hear the mellow wedding bells” is a plain case. The words mellow, wedding and bells all carry the short e of “bed”. Listen with your ears, because spelling misleads. The long i of “time” is spelled differently in “sigh”, and the two still echo each other.

afterFigure.text: Set alliteration beside assonance and the difference is clear. Alliteration catches the ear at the start of words, and assonance catches it in the middle, so alliteration tends to tap and assonance tends to hum. Shakespeare's line “And with old woes new wail my dear time's waste” uses vowel echoes twice, old with woes and wail with waste.

steps.headline: Count the long i sounds in Keats's “Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness”.

lead.text: Assonance follows the sound of a vowel, whatever the spelling. Say each word aloud.

reveal.text: The long vowel of “bride” returns in “quietness”, which ties the bride to the quiet she belongs to. Pictures are the next thing a line can build.

steps.headline: From the ear to the eye

lead.text: Sound is half of what a line does. The other half is the picture it puts in your head, and the simplest way to make a picture is to compare one thing with another. Suppose you are describing a noisy classroom. You could say “The classroom was like a zoo.” The word “like” announces the comparison and keeps the two things apart, so the room resembles a zoo. A comparison made with “like” or “as” is called a simile.

You could also drop the word and say “The classroom was a zoo.” Now nothing keeps the two things apart. The sentence says that one thing is the other, and it can carry on from there: the teacher is the keeper and the children are the animals. A comparison that says one thing is another, with no “like” or “as”, is a metaphor. The reader knows the room is not really a zoo, and the claim does its work anyway.

afterFigure.text: The two forms often carry the same picture and differ in strength. A simile asks you to hold two things side by side, and a metaphor asks you to see one through the other. To tell them apart, look for “like” or “as”.

lead.text: Burns writes “O my Luve's like a red, red rose.” Look for the word that tells you how the comparison is made.

reveal.text: “Like” keeps the two things apart, so the line is a simile. Every comparison has two parts, and the next screen names them.

spans.text: And all the men and women merely players

lead.text: Every comparison has two parts. In “The classroom was a zoo” the thing being described is the classroom. The thing borrowed to describe it is the zoo. The critic I. A. Richards gave them names in 1936: the subject is the tenor and the borrowed picture is the vehicle. The tenor is what the line is about, and the vehicle carries a set of qualities across to it, here noise, mess and animals let loose.

In Burns's line love is the tenor and the rose is the vehicle. The rose carries freshness and colour across to the love. Sometimes the vehicle is never named. “The committee chair growled and snapped at every question” says nothing about a dog. The growling and snapping describe one anyway, so the reader supplies it. The details alone point to the vehicle.

afterFigure.text: To read a figure, find what the line is about and what picture has been borrowed. The qualities that travel from one to the other are the point of the figure.

lead.text: Dickinson writes “Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul”. Her tenor is hope. She does not name the vehicle in these lines, but the details point to it.

reveal.text: The details add up to one creature, and the second stanza names it. Naming tenor and vehicle lets you say exactly what a figure carries across.

spans.text: Hope is the thing with feathers

blocks.text: A tongue-twister such as “she sells seashells on the seashore” is hard to say five times without a slip. The words are short and the meaning is plain. What trips you is that the same few sounds keep turning up close together, and your mouth has to switch between them faster than it comfortably can.

Poets know that closeness of sound works on the ear in the same way, only more gently. A cluster of one sound can hush a line or make it rattle. Sound is only half of what a line does, though. The other half is the picture it puts in your head, which poets often build by saying that one thing is another.
This lesson follows both halves. It starts with sound, consonants first and then vowels, and then turns to pictures, with lines from Shakespeare, Keats, Burns and Dickinson along the way.

lessons.title: The sonnet and its turn

lead.text: Two words rhyme when they end on the same sound, as day and way do. In a poem the rhymes sit at the ends of lines, and the way they are arranged is the poem's rhyme scheme. To write a scheme down, give each new end-sound a letter in order of appearance and reuse the letter whenever the sound comes back. The first line ends on a sound we call A. If the second line ends on a different sound, that is B. If the third line rhymes with the first, it is A again.

Thomas Gray's “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard” begins: “The curfew tolls the knell of parting day, / The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea, / The plowman homeward plods his weary way, / And leaves the world to darkness and to me.” The line endings are day, lea, way and me. Day and way rhyme, and lea and me rhyme, so the scheme reads ABAB. A group of four lines like this is called a quatrain, from the French word for four. Each of Gray's lines is also iambic pentameter, the ten-syllable line you met in the last lesson.

Once the endings have letters you can compare patterns at a glance. ABAB means that lines one and three rhyme with each other and lines two and four rhyme with each other. A line that rhymes with nothing takes a letter of its own.
Say the four lines of the rhyme aloud and listen to the last word of each line.

steps.headline: A poem that changes its mind

lead.text: A sonnet is short enough to hold one argument, and most sonnets argue something. They set out a problem, a doubt or a complaint. At some point they turn. The speaker finds an answer or a comfort, or comes to doubt what was just said. The turn is called the volta, which is the Italian word for it. A small word such as but, yet or and yet often signals it.

Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 begins by asking whether it is fair to compare someone to a summer's day. The first eight lines say that the person is lovelier than summer and give the reasons: summer has rough winds, a short lease, a sun that is sometimes too hot and sometimes dimmed. Then line 9 begins “But thy eternal summer shall not fade”, and the poem changes direction. The person praised will outlast any season, because the poem itself will keep them alive.
The turn gives a sonnet its direction. The next screens look at how the fourteen lines are laid out around it, which depends on which of two forms the poet chose.

Here is the shape of Sonnet 18 itself. It has fourteen lines of iambic pentameter, and they fall into four groups. The first twelve make three quatrains. The first rhymes ABAB, the second CDCD and the third EFEF, so each brings in two new rhyme sounds. The last two lines make a couplet, a pair of rhyming lines, and the couplet adds one more sound, G. The whole scheme is ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.

Look at the figure. The rhyme sounds are printed beside each line, and the tag on line 9 marks the volta from the last screen. Notice how the form helps the argument. Each quatrain has room for one step of the case. The first two deal with summer's faults and the third turns to the promise of permanence. The couplet then closes the argument, like a signature at the foot of a letter.

afterFigure.text: This is the Shakespearean sonnet, which is also called the English sonnet. The form suited English well, because it asks for seven different rhyme sounds and each sound is needed only twice. The older Italian form is more demanding, and it is where we go next.

lines.text: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
Let me not to the marriage of true minds
Admit impediments. Love is not love
Which alters when it alteration finds,
Or bends with the remover to remove:
O no! it is an ever-fixed mark
That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
It is the star to every wandering bark,
Whose worth’s unknown, although his height be taken.
Love’s not Time’s fool, though rosy lips and cheeks
Within his bending sickle’s compass come;
Love alters not with his brief hours and weeks,
But bears it out even to the edge of doom.
If this be error and upon me proved,
I never writ, nor no man ever loved.

lead.text: Each quatrain of a Shakespearean sonnet brings rhymes of its own, and the couplet answers them. Sonnet 18 ends: “So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.”

reveal.text: Seven, A to G. Each quatrain brings two new rhymes and the couplet adds one, so the poem moves through seven sounds and ends on a pair.

lead.text: Shakespeare's pattern is not the only one. The sonnet began in Italy in the 1200s, and the poet Petrarch, writing in the 1300s, made it famous. His pattern splits the fourteen lines into two unequal parts. The first eight lines are the octave and the last six are the sestet. The octave sets out a problem or a feeling, and the sestet answers it.

The octave's rhyme scheme is strict: ABBAABBA. The sound that ends line 1 comes back in lines 4, 5 and 8, and the sound that ends line 2 comes back in lines 3, 6 and 7. Italian has many words that end alike, so the pattern is manageable there. English has fewer, so an English poet who keeps to it is working hard. John Milton does in his sonnet on going blind, which begins “When I consider how my light is spent”. The sestet that follows is looser, and poets have several patterns for it.

The two forms divide the fourteen lines differently. Shakespeare's runs as three groups of four and a pair, and Petrarch's as a group of eight and a group of six. The division matters because the turn tends to fall at a join. In Petrarch's form that is the join between octave and sestet, after line 8. In Shakespeare's it can fall at line 9, the start of the third quatrain. It can also fall at the couplet.

lead.text: Sonnet 29 spends its opening quatrains on envy and self-pity. Read for the first word that changes direction, and count down to its line.

lines.text: When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes
I all alone beweep my outcast state,
And trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries,
And look upon myself, and curse my fate,
Wishing me like to one more rich in hope,
Featur’d like him, like him with friends possess’d,
Desiring this man’s art, and that man’s scope,
With what I most enjoy contented least;
Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising,
Haply I think on thee, and then my state,
Like to the lark at break of day arising
From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven’s gate;
For thy sweet love remember’d such wealth brings
That then I scorn to change my state with kings.

steps.headline: A turn saved for the end

lead.text: So far the turn has come at the start of a new section, at line 9 where a third quatrain begins or at the join in Milton's form. Shakespeare could also hold it back until the couplet. Then three whole quatrains build a case, and the last two lines overturn it or twist it. The reader has settled into one attitude by then, and the couplet pulls the floor away.

Where the turn falls decides how a poem feels. An early turn leaves most of the poem for the answer. A late turn leaves most of it for the problem, and the couplet carries a surprise. To find a volta, look for the point where the speaker's attitude shifts and count the lines up to it. Words such as but, yet and and yet are often the sign.
Sonnet 130 spends its quatrains mocking the flattering comparisons that love poets usually make. Read the lines and decide where the mockery stops.

reveal.text: The couplet carries the turn: “And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare”. Milton turns early, in line 8: “But patience to prevent / That murmur, soon replies”. Where the turn falls decides how much of the poem argues and how much answers.

lines.text: My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red, than her lips red:
If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;
If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
I have seen roses damask’d, red and white,
But no such roses see I in her cheeks;
And in some perfumes is there more delight
Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.
I love to hear her speak, yet well I know
That music hath a far more pleasing sound:
I grant I never saw a goddess go;
My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:
And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare,
As any she belied with false compare.
When I consider how my light is spent,
E’re half my days, in this dark world and wide,
And that one Talent which is death to hide,

To serve therewith my Maker, and present
My true account, least he returning chide,
Doth God exact day-labour, light deny’d,
I fondly ask; But patience to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, God doth not need
Either man’s work or his own gifts, who best
Bear his milde yoak, they serve him best, his State
Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest:
They also serve who only stand and waite.
