blocks.text: Most people know the rhyme that begins “Roses are red”. Say it aloud and you can feel its shape without trying. The lines come in a set of four, and two of them end on the same sound, which gives the little verse a click at the end, like a door closing.

That click is the effect a poet is after in a much larger form, the sonnet. A sonnet is a poem of fourteen lines, and poets have used the form for more than seven centuries, for love poems and for arguments with God. Its rhymes follow a fixed pattern, and somewhere along the way the poem usually changes its mind.

This lesson builds a sonnet up from the rhyme you already know. You learn how to write a rhyme pattern as letters, how a sonnet is divided and how to find the line where it turns. The poems are by Shakespeare and Milton.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a sonnet's rhyme scheme and find the line where its argument turns.

recap.keyIdea: A sonnet has a fixed rhyme pattern and a turn. The volta is where the poem answers its own problem, early in Petrarch's form and often late in Shakespeare's.

blocks.text: You found seven rhyme sounds in Shakespeare's scheme and two in Milton's octave, and you placed the turns of Sonnets 29 and 130 at lines 9 and 13. The little rhyme you began with works on the same principle, with end-sounds that pair lines up.

recap.nextHook: Poems are only one way to tell a story. The next lesson begins with a friend retelling an awkward entrance twice, once as “I” and once as “she”. It asks who is speaking.

lessons.title: Who sees and who speaks

lead.text: The person who tells a story is its narrator, and the first thing to settle about any narrator is where they stand. Go back to the two friends. The one who says “I walked in” is inside the story and is one of its characters. Narration like this is in the first person, because the pronouns are I and we. Edgar Allan Poe's narrator in “The Tell-Tale Heart” works this way: “why will you say that I am mad?”

The friend who says “she walked in” stands outside, watching. That is the third person, because the people in the story are he, she and they. Jane Austen's Persuasion opens this way: “Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own amusement, never took up any book but the Baronetage.” Nobody says “I” there, and the narrator is not one of the Elliots. A rarer choice is the second person, which speaks to the reader as “you”, as in “You walk in and everyone goes quiet”.

afterFigure.text: The pronouns give the quickest test. Look at the words a narrator uses for themselves and for the characters. If the narrator says I or we, they are inside the story. If they never mention themselves and call the characters he, she or they, they stand outside it.

spans.text: had been and am; but why will you say that
Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own amusement, never took up any book but the Baronetage;

lead.text: Emma begins with a narrator describing its heroine. Read the opening and notice whether the narrator ever speaks as a character or stays outside.

reveal.text: Third person: the narrator names Emma and calls her “she”. The word “seemed” already hints that this narrator has a wider view than Emma, which is the next idea.

spans.text: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence;
True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?

lead.text: A third-person narrator can stay close to one character or stand well back. The widest position belongs to the omniscient narrator, from the Latin for “all-knowing”. An omniscient narrator can see into every mind, say what happened before the story began and comment on what it all means. Take an invented line: “Everyone in Little Wick knew that the new vicar would not last the winter, though he himself was sure he would.” The narrator knows what a whole village thinks and what the vicar believes, and the two do not match.

That wide view lets a narrator speak as though for everyone while quietly standing apart. A narrator can state a belief that belongs to a community and let the reader notice that the narrator does not share it. The sentence reports the village's certainty in the village's confident voice, and its second half shows how little the vicar knows. The tone is dry. That dryness is a kind of irony, where the words say one thing and the situation suggests another, and a later lesson looks at it properly.

afterFigure.text: An omniscient narrator is not always the author speaking plainly. It can voice a community's assumption, state a general truth with a straight face and leave the reader to judge. When a novel opens with a confident statement about what everybody knows, ask whose belief it is.

spans.text: Everyone in Little Wick knew that the new vicar would not last the winter,
though he himself was sure he would.
The whole street had decided that the new family was too grand to speak to,
though the family had only been waiting for someone to speak first.

lead.text: Pride and Prejudice opens with a claim about what is “universally acknowledged”. Ask who is speaking, and whose assumption it is.

reveal.text: The narrator voices a neighbourhood's assumption with irony. The next paragraph shows the “surrounding families” regarding a rich newcomer as “the rightful property” of their daughters, so the wanting runs the other way.

spans.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged,
that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.
this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as
of some one or other of their daughters.

lead.text: A narrator has a choice about how to report what a character thinks. Suppose Ben opens the oven and finds that his cake has sunk. The simplest way is to quote him in his own words and his own person: “This cake is a disaster!” That is direct speech, and the quotation marks show that the words belong to Ben. Another way is to report the thought from outside: Ben thought that the cake was a disaster. Now the narrator is in charge, and the thought arrives wrapped in “Ben thought that”.

There is a third way, which sits between the two. The narrator keeps the third person and the past tense but lets Ben's own exclamation into the sentence, and drops the reporting words: The cake was a disaster! No quotation marks and no “thought that” announce the change. The voice is the narrator's and the feeling is Ben's. Writers call this free indirect discourse. Words that only the character would use, such as an exclamation or a bit of slang, give it away.

afterFigure.text: Turning a direct thought into this form takes two changes. The person moves from I to he or she, and the tense moves back a step, so that “I have no time!” becomes “She had no time!” The exclamation and the choice of words stay the character's own. Because nothing signals the switch, the reader slides into the character's mind without noticing the join.

spans.text: Ben thought that the cake was a disaster.
Ana thought that she would never get a seat.
She would never get a seat!

steps.headline: Turn Anna's thought “What a dreadful day this has been!” into free indirect discourse.

lead.text: Apply the two changes from the last screen to a new sentence. Follow each move.

workedSteps.text: Start from the direct thought, in her words and her person: “What a dreadful day this has been!”
Move to the narrator's grammar: third person and past tense.
Keep her exclamation and drop the reporting words. “What a dreadful day it had been!”

lead.text: After Mr Elton's proposal, Austen writes: “Emma sat down to think and be miserable. It was a wretched business indeed!” The second sentence is Emma's own exclamation.

reveal.text: The narrator's grammar carries Emma's voice, so readers share her mistakes before they recognise them as mistakes.

spans.text: The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
It was a wretched business indeed!
Ben thought that the cake was a disaster.

lead.text: Any line of a narrative can be sorted with two checks: who is speaking, and whose words they are. Quotation marks mark direct speech, where the words are the character's own. Actions and facts reported from outside, with no character's voice in them, are plain narration. The case in between, where the narrator's grammar carries a character's voice, is free indirect discourse. In the figure, Mia hangs up her coat, her father asks where she has been, and then comes a line in her voice but the narrator's grammar.

The effect matters as much as the label. In free indirect discourse the reader hears a character's mind with no narrator standing between. When the character is mistaken, the reader can take on the mistake along with them. Austen uses this in Emma, where we share Emma's confident reading of other people and discover only later that she has misjudged them.

afterFigure.text: A narrator who can be inside a mind and outside it at once can show how a character sees things and how things are. The gap between the two is where a writer can be funny or unsettling, and it leads into the next lesson.

spans.text: “Where have you been?” asked her father.
Honestly, what a day it had been!

lead.text: Use the two sorting questions on three sentences from Emma. Quotation marks mark direct speech. Actions reported from outside are plain narration. One sentence carries Emma's voice in the narrator's grammar.

reveal.text: “How she could have been so deceived!” is Emma's exclamation in the narrator's third person and past tense. No reporting verb or quotation marks frame it.

spans.text: (1) “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
(2) The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
(3) How she could have been so deceived!
Such an overthrow of every thing she had been wishing for!
She looked back as well as she could;

blocks.text: Two friends are telling you about the same awkward entrance. Yesterday one of them walked into a meeting twenty minutes late, and the whole room turned to look. The first friend says: “I walked in and everyone went quiet.” The second, who watched from the corner, says: “She walked in and everyone went quiet.”

The event is identical and the two accounts feel different. The first puts you inside the person who walked in, feeling the heat in her face. The second puts you across the room, watching her. A story always comes from somewhere, and where the teller stands decides what you can see, what you can know and how far you can trust it.

This lesson is about that choice, which writers call point of view. It starts with the simplest question, who is telling, and works up to a trick Jane Austen used to let readers hear a character's thoughts without leaving the voice of the person telling the story.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell first- from third-person narration and spot free indirect discourse in Austen.

recap.keyIdea: A narrator's grammatical person fixes where they stand. Free indirect discourse lets a character's own voice speak inside the narrator's third person.

blocks.text: You sorted narrators by whether they say “I”, and you heard an omniscient narrator voice a whole village's assumption. You turned a direct thought into free indirect discourse and picked out Emma's exclamation among three sentences. The two friends at the start turned out to be using the first and the third person.

recap.nextHook: A narrator can say one thing and mean another. The next lesson looks at irony, and at how a reader decides whether a narrator can be trusted.

lessons.title: Irony and unreliable narrators

steps.headline: A remark that means the opposite

lead.text: Go back to the customer with soup in his lap. What he said was “Lovely, thank you.” What he meant was close to the reverse. When someone says one thing and means another, and the listener can hear the difference, we call the result irony. This first kind lives in the speaker’s words, so it is called verbal irony.

The difference only counts if it can be heard. A stranger who knew nothing about the soup would take the remark at face value, and the joke would vanish. What makes it audible is the scene, since everyone present can see the stain and so can measure how far the words fall from the facts. Tone of voice helps, though a page has no tone and there the scene is all a reader has.

afterFigure.text: So verbal irony needs two things, a statement that points one way and a situation that points the other. Take either away and what is left is a plain remark. That suggests a question about how far the idea can stretch. A single sentence can set up a gap, and a speaker could also build one slowly, over a whole speech. The next screen follows one who did.

model.speaker: The customer
model.said: The soup was lovely and he is grateful.
model.known: Soup has just landed in his lap, and everyone in the room can see it.

model.speaker: A commuter
model.line: I do love standing in a queue.
model.known: She has stood in the rain for forty minutes, and so has everyone around her.

lead.text: Here is a similar scene with one detail changed. A friend has laid out a picnic on the grass. Rain starts to fall, and she watches it soak the sandwiches.

reveal.text: She means the opposite of what she says. As with the soup, the scene supplies the gap: sodden sandwiches and a cheerful remark do not fit together.

lead.text: Verbal irony does not have to stay inside one sentence. Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar has one of the best-known examples. Caesar has been murdered by a group of Roman senators led by Brutus, who tells the crowd that Caesar was ambitious and had to die for Rome’s sake. Mark Antony, Caesar’s friend, is allowed to speak at the funeral on one condition: he must not speak against the killers. So he does not. He praises them.

Antony keeps coming back to one phrase. Brutus says Caesar was ambitious, he tells the crowd, “and Brutus is an honourable man.” Then he offers some facts. Caesar brought captives home whose ransoms filled Rome’s treasury, and when a crown was held out to him he refused it three times. After each fact, the phrase returns.

afterFigure.text: The words never change, yet they come to mean something else. The first time, “honourable” sounds like respect. After the ransoms and the refused crown it sounds like an accusation, and the crowd supplies the meaning. Antony never calls Brutus a liar. The evidence builds the gap between what he says and what the crowd now believes, and the repetition makes sure nobody misses it. In the lines that follow, see how often he returns to the phrase.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: For Brutus is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, so his charge against Caesar must be true.
model.known: The crowd still trusts Brutus, so the line sounds like respect.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: And sure he is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, so his charge against Caesar must be true.
model.known: The crowd has heard about the ransoms and the refused crown, and now hears the opposite.

lead.text: Below are eight lines from the speech. Brutus is named in several of them, and one phrase is used to describe him. Count how often it is applied to Brutus himself.

reveal.text: Four times. Each repetition follows evidence against the charge of ambition, so by the last one the word has turned against Brutus, and the crowd has done the turning.

spans.text: So are they all, all honourable men,
But Brutus says he was ambitious,
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: For Brutus is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, and so his charge that Caesar was ambitious must be true.
model.known: Brutus helped kill Caesar, and each repetition invites the crowd to doubt the word.

lead.text: Verbal irony needs a speaker who means the opposite. There is another kind of gap that needs no such speaker, and a story most people know shows it. Little Red Riding Hood reaches her grandmother’s bed and says, “What big teeth you have!” She is making a polite remark about her grandmother. The audience knows that the figure in the bed is the wolf, so every word she speaks carries a meaning she cannot hear.

That is dramatic irony. The audience, or the reader, knows something that a character does not, and the character’s words or actions take on a meaning the character cannot see. The name comes from drama, because the stage is where it works best. A theatre audience has watched the whole story and sits in the dark knowing more than anyone on stage, and a playwright can use that edge by letting a hero walk cheerfully towards a trap.

afterFigure.text: Nobody in Red Riding Hood’s scene says the opposite of what they mean. The gap lies between what the character knows and what we know, and it widens the longer the character stays in the dark. That makes it a favourite of tragedy, where the audience often knows how the story ends before the hero does. The next screen goes to one of the best-known cases, in a tomb.

model.speaker: Little Red Riding Hood
model.said: A polite remark about her grandmother’s teeth.
model.known: The figure in the bed is the wolf, and the audience has seen it swallow the grandmother.

model.speaker: The detective
model.line: I would trust Hobbs with my life.
model.known: The audience saw Hobbs slip the silver into his coat.

lead.text: Romeo finds Juliet lying in her family’s tomb and believes she is dead. He says that death has had no power yet over her beauty.

reveal.text: Dramatic irony. Every line Romeo speaks means more to us than to him. Duncan’s “This castle hath a pleasant seat” works the same way, spoken by a king the audience knows will be murdered inside it.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: Death that hath suck’d the honey of thy breath, / Hath had no power yet upon thy beauty.
model.said: Juliet is dead, and her beauty is death's strange mercy.
model.known: Juliet has taken the Friar's sleeping potion and is about to wake.

model.speaker: Duncan
model.line: This castle hath a pleasant seat.
model.said: The castle is a welcoming place to rest.
model.known: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth have resolved to murder Duncan there that night.

steps.headline: When events turn on their maker

lead.text: The third gap lies in nobody’s words and nobody’s knowledge. It lies in what happens. In O. Henry’s short story “The Gift of the Magi”, a poor young couple want to give each other something special at Christmas. Della sells her long hair to buy a chain for her husband Jim’s treasured watch. When she gets home, Jim gives her a set of combs for her hair. He has sold the watch to pay for them.

Each gift was chosen out of love, and each has been made useless by the other’s sacrifice. Nobody says the opposite of what they mean, and nobody knows more than the others when the choices are made. The irony comes from the outcome, which reverses what both of them intended. That is situational irony: an event that turns against the purpose that set it going.

afterFigure.text: Situational irony turns up outside stories too. A safety inspector who trips over a loose rug during her own inspection is a small example. To spot it, ask what the event was meant to achieve and whether it did the reverse. If it did, and nobody is speaking or knowing differently, the gap is in the situation. That makes three places where the gap can sit, and a story has one more.

model.source: O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi
model.speaker: Della and Jim
model.line: Combs for her hair, bought with his watch, and a chain for his watch, bought with her hair.
model.said: Each gift is a treat for the one they love.
model.known: Each has sold the thing the other’s gift was meant for, so neither gift can be used.

model.speaker: A safety inspector
model.line: She trips over a loose rug during her own inspection.
model.said: She is there to find hazards and keep people safe.
model.known: She is the one who falls over a hazard she failed to see.

lead.text: In Act 3 of Romeo and Juliet, two men are fighting. Romeo steps between them to make peace. Tybalt thrusts under Romeo’s arm and kills his friend Mercutio.

reveal.text: Situational irony. The outcome turns against its cause: peace-making gives Tybalt his opening. This kind needs no speaker and no hidden knowledge, only an outcome that reverses its purpose.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: I thought all for the best.
model.said: Stepping between the fighters will stop the duel.
model.known: Tybalt's thrust under Romeo's arm kills Mercutio: the peace-making makes the death possible.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: And sure he is an honourable man.
model.known: Antony means the opposite, and the crowd hears it.

lead.text: Three statements follow, and they mix the kinds you have met. For each one, ask who knows what, and whether an outcome has turned against its purpose.

reveal.text: Two. Statements 1 and 3 give the audience knowledge a character lacks. Statement 2 is an outcome that reverses an expectation, so it is situational.

steps.headline: A narrator who gives himself away

lead.text: The last place a gap can open is in the narrator. In the last lesson you met narrators who tell a story in the first person, and so far we have taken their word for what happened. Often we should. But a narrator can say one thing about himself while his own telling shows another, and then the reader has to notice. Suppose a narrator says: “I have never been calmer in my life. I counted the spoons three times to be sure.” He insists on calm, and the counting says otherwise.

A narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt is an unreliable narrator. The critic Wayne Booth gave the idea its name in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961). The narrator need not be lying. He may be deluded, biased, too close to events or simply wrong. What matters is that the evidence against his account comes from inside his own telling, in protests that are too loud, details that clash with his claims and sentences that break apart as he speaks.

afterFigure.text: That is how you read past such a narrator. You collect what he lets slip and build a second story behind his version, and the distance between the two stories is the gap. It is the same kind of gap as before, between what is said and what the facts show. The only difference is that here the facts have to be pieced together from the narrator’s own words.

spans.text: I have never been calmer in my life.
I counted the spoons three times to be sure, and I locked the door, and then I checked the lock again.
“and the icing was already on my chin when I found it.”

lead.text: Poe’s narrator in “The Tell-Tale Heart” has killed an old man. In these lines he argues that he cannot be mad. Look at how he argues, as well as what he says.

reveal.text: The reader learns to doubt the account from evidence inside the telling, and assembles a second story from what the narrator lets slip.

spans.text: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am;
but why will you say that I am mad?
I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell.
Object there was none. Passion there was none.

blocks.text: A waiter tips a bowl of soup into a customer’s lap. The customer looks down at the stain spreading across his trousers and says, in a calm voice, “Lovely, thank you.” Nobody at the next table thinks he is pleased, and the waiter, scarlet in the face, understands at once.

That small exchange holds something you will meet in plays, in stories and in everyday talk. The customer’s words and the situation point in opposite directions, and the listeners notice the space between them. Sometimes a speaker means the opposite of the words on purpose. Sometimes it opens because the audience knows something a character does not, or because events turn against the person who set them going.
This lesson follows that gap as it widens. It starts with the spilt soup and moves onto the stage. It ends with a narrator who tells you one thing and, without meaning to, shows you another.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll tell three kinds of irony apart and read past a narrator who gives himself away.

recap.keyIdea: Irony is a gap between what is said, known or intended and what actually comes out. It can open in a speaker’s words, in the audience’s knowledge, in the way events turn or in a narrator’s account of himself.

blocks.text: You began with a man and a spilt bowl of soup and heard the same gap grow into Antony’s speech, where one phrase meant the opposite by the fourth time. You saw Romeo in the tomb as dramatic irony and his peace-making as situational irony, and you sorted three statements by who knows what. At the end you read past Poe’s narrator, whose protests of calm gave him away.

recap.nextHook: Every one of those gaps sits in a particular scene, and where the scene falls changes how a story feels. The next lesson maps a play scene by scene and finds the point where it reaches its height.

lessons.title: Structure: arcs and turning scenes

lead.text: Go back to the film and its marks out of ten. Write the marks in a row and draw a line through them, and the line behaves like a walk across hilly ground. It starts low and climbs for most of the way. Then it reaches a summit and comes down on the other side. The sketch below does this for two stories you may know, with one bar for each scene.

afterFigure.text: The summit is the climax, the point where a story reaches its greatest height. Before it, the fortunes of the main character, who is called the protagonist, are mostly climbing. After it they fall. Finding the climax is the first skill in this lesson, and it needs only two moves. Read the height of each scene, then pick the highest.
In everyday speech a climax can mean any exciting moment. Here the word has a narrower sense. It means the top of the hill, and a story has only one.

model.title: Little Red Riding Hood in six scenes

lead.text: Here is a film scored the way the opener described, with one mark out of ten for each of five scenes. Use the summit test from the last screen.

reveal.text: Scene 4 scores 9, the highest mark. After it the tension eases to 5, so the film reaches its peak in the fourth scene and falls away.

lead.text: In 1863 the German writer Gustav Freytag studied how the plays of ancient Greece and of Shakespeare were put together, and described the pattern he found in a five-act play. He drew it as a pyramid, which is the hill from the last screen with straight sides. The pyramid has five parts, and each has a name.

The first part sets out the world before anything happens, with its place, its time and its people. Freytag called it the introduction, and English critics usually call it the exposition. Next comes the rising action, a run of events in which the protagonist’s fortunes climb and the trouble tightens. At the top sits the climax. After the climax, the falling action carries events downhill until the play ends in the catastrophe, the final stroke that settles the protagonist’s fate.

afterFigure.text: “Catastrophe” sounds like a disaster, and in a tragedy it is, because the hero falls. In other kinds of story the same place in the pyramid is called the resolution or the denouement, and it may be a happy one. A comedy, for example, rises again at its end towards a wedding or a reunion. The five names hold for every plot, and they let you say where in a story any event belongs.

model.title: Red Riding Hood, named by part

scenes.label: Rising: the wolf in the wood

lead.text: One part of the pyramid comes before any conflict starts. In Romeo and Juliet it would hold an Italian city where swords are worn and quarrels flare, ruled by a prince who keeps the peace with difficulty.

reveal.text: The exposition, which Freytag called the introduction. It sets out the world before the action starts and ends when something disturbs it, such as Romeo and his friends deciding to go to the Capulet feast.

steps.headline: Romeo and Juliet in five acts

lead.text: Freytag applied his pyramid to Shakespeare, so Romeo and Juliet makes a good test. In Act 1 two families, the Montagues and the Capulets, are at feud. Romeo, a Montague, goes uninvited to a Capulet feast and falls in love with Juliet. In Act 2 they meet again in a garden at night and are secretly married the next day.

Act 3 begins with a street fight in which Tybalt, Juliet’s cousin, kills Romeo’s friend Mercutio. Romeo kills Tybalt in revenge, and the prince banishes him from the city. The newly married lovers have one night together before he must leave. Their luck has been climbing since the feast.

In Act 4 Juliet is told to marry another man, and she takes a drink from Friar Laurence that will make her seem dead for more than a day. In Act 5 a message to Romeo goes astray. He hears that she is dead and dies beside her in the tomb, and Juliet wakes to find him gone and takes her own life. Read the story with the pyramid in mind. Everything before the climax climbs, and everything after it falls.
Freytag counted the play’s five acts and put one of them at the top of his pyramid. Use the story you have just read to say which.

reveal.text: Act 3. Freytag traces the rise through the masked ball, the garden, the wedding and Tybalt’s death. He sets the climax in Act 3, from Juliet’s “Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds” to Romeo’s farewell. Everything after it descends towards the tomb.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

lead.text: The pyramid works act by act. A closer look goes scene by scene and asks something different: has this scene changed anything for the protagonist? To answer, give each scene a value, either hope (+) or loss (−), at its start and again at its end. A scene might begin with the lovers hopeful and end with one of them banished.

When a scene ends on a different value from the one it began with, it is a turning scene: it has turned the story from hope to loss or from loss to hope. Where the two values match, the scene builds or confirms what was already so. A balcony meeting that begins in hope and ends in more hope has turned nothing, even if it moves us.

afterFigure.text: In the sketch above, Cinderella has three turning scenes. The fairy godmother turns loss into hope. Midnight turns it back, and the slipper hunt reverses it again. Red Riding Hood has two. Counting turning scenes shows where a story is busiest. A play in which every scene turned would be exhausting, and one in which none did would stand still.

model.title: Little Red Riding Hood in six scenes

lead.text: Here is the same test on bare signs. Each scene is written as its opening value, then its closing value.

reveal.text: Two. The first scene turns hope into loss and the second turns loss into hope. The third opens and closes at +, so it holds.

lead.text: The figure gives eight scenes of Romeo and Juliet, with the lovers’ value at the start and end of each. Apply the same test to every scene.

reveal.text: Five of the eight turn. The tomb opens in loss and stays there, and the balcony and the wedding hold their hope.

lead.text: Look again at the eight scenes you just checked. The five that turn are not spread evenly. The feast turns loss into hope, and then the lovers hold their hope through the balcony and the wedding. After the wedding the turns come thick and fast, four in the second half of the play.

Put this beside the pyramid and the two views agree. The climax in Act 3 sits where those turns begin, and the falling action is the stretch in which they keep coming. The pyramid names the parts of the shape, and the turning scenes show what the shape is made of: one change after another in the protagonists’ fortunes.

Both tests work on a story you have never read. Score the scenes and find the highest, then read the signs to see where the story changes. The last question asks for the first of these on a heist film.
Here is a story you have not met, a heist film in six scenes. The bars show how far the action has climbed in each one. Apply the first test, and give the scene’s number counting from the left.

reveal.text: Scene 4, the alarm. The chase and the split are falling action, and the last scene works as the catastrophe or resolution. Comedies use the same shape with the ending reversed, rising again to a marriage or a reunion.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

lessons.orientation: Map a play onto Freytag's pyramid, find its climax, and count the scenes that turn a value from hope to loss or back.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Think of a film you know well and lay its scenes out in order, the way chapters sit on a shelf. Now give each scene a mark out of ten for how tense it is. The marks will not be random. The opening scenes usually score low and the middle ones climb, and somewhere near the end there is a scene that scores higher than all the rest.

Not every story builds in the same way, yet nearly all of them have a shape that can be drawn. A plot rises, reaches a high point and falls away. The shape tells you which scene matters most and how long the story takes to wind down after it.

This lesson draws that shape for a play. It starts with a simple way to score a story and goes on to the names a nineteenth-century German critic gave to its parts. It ends by checking which scenes of Romeo and Juliet change the lovers’ luck.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll find the high point of a plot, name its parts and count the scenes that change a story’s course.

recap.keyIdea: A plot climbs to a highest point and falls away. Freytag’s pyramid names the parts, and the scenes whose value changes show where the story moves.

blocks.text: You found the tensest of five film scenes and placed the climax of Romeo and Juliet in Act 3. You counted five turning scenes among its eight and found the alarm as the climax of a heist in six scenes. The film you scored at the start turned out to have the same hill-shaped outline as the plays.

recap.nextHook: You now have the tools to read a sentence, an argument, a poem and a story. Pick a text of your own and try them on it.

questions.prompt: Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 says 'And every fair from fair sometime declines.' Which single word is the finite verb?
hints: Which test from the last screen can you use? Put the line into the past.
Say the line with “once” in front and listen for the word that has to change.
A verb in the past often ends in -ed. Which word could take that ending?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Declines' is the finite verb: it carries tense and would become 'declined' in the past. Its subject is 'every fair'.

questions.onCorrect: “Declines” is the finite verb: in the past it would become “declined”.

misconceptions.feedback: That word names what is changing or says when. Put the line into the past and see which word has to change.

questions.prompt: In 'Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May', the object is a noun phrase. What is its head noun, the one word the rest of the phrase describes?
hints: Strip away the describing words. Which noun is left as the thing being shaken?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The object is 'the darling buds of May'; its head noun is 'buds'. 'Darling' and 'of May' modify it.

questions.onCorrect: The head of “the darling buds of May” is “buds”. “Darling” and “of May” only describe it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Darling” describes the noun. Find the noun that the other words are describing.
“May” sits inside “of May”, which describes the thing shaken rather than naming it.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 130 has 'If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun.' Which word makes the first clause dependent?
hints: Which word turns a statement into a condition?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'If' subordinates 'snow be white', so that clause cannot stand alone; 'her breasts are dun' can.

questions.onCorrect: “If” turns “snow be white” into a condition, so that clause cannot stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the clause's own content. Look for the small word in front that makes it wait for an answer.

questions.prompt: How many finite verbs are in 'Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds'?
hints: A finite verb carries tense: test each word by putting the lines into the past.
Check the main clause, then the clause opened by 'which', then the clause opened by 'when'.
List one verb from each clause and count the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'is', 'alters' and 'finds'. Each anchors a clause.

questions.onCorrect: Three: “is”, “alters” and “finds”. Each finite verb anchors its own clause.

misconceptions.feedback: Two clauses are easy to see, but the clause opened by “when” has a verb of its own.
That counts only the main clause. The clauses opened by “which” and “when” each have a verb.
Check that every word you counted carries tense. A noun is not a verb.

questions.prompt: Douglass, 1852: 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' How many independent clauses does this sentence hold?
hints: Find each subject and finite verb pair.
Ask whether each clause could stand as a sentence on its own.
Neither clause opens with a subordinator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'You may rejoice' and 'I must mourn'. Each could stand alone, and the comma between them is a deliberate splice.

questions.onCorrect: Two: “You may rejoice” and “I must mourn”. Each has its own subject and verb and could stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a second subject with its own verb. A comma does not fuse two clauses into one.
Pair each subject with its finite verb. “May” and “must” belong to the verbs beside them.

questions.prompt: In Lincoln's 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here', what is the grammatical function of 'what we say here'?
hints: Ask: the world will little note what? The answer names the object.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'What we say here' is a noun clause that receives the action of 'note' and 'remember', so it is their object. The subject is 'the world'.

questions.onCorrect: “What we say here” is what the world will note and remember, so it is the object of both verbs.

misconceptions.feedback: The subject does the noting. Ask what is noted: that is the clause in question.
A complement follows a linking verb and describes the subject. “Note” and “remember” act on something.

questions.prompt: 'The vote was close, the motion failed.' Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone. What do editors call this construction?
hints: Look at what separates the two halves, and at whether each half could stand alone.
The name pairs the mark with a word from rope-work and film editing.
Joining two lengths of rope or film end to end is called splicing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comma splice: in edited prose a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.onCorrect: A comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses in edited prose.

misconceptions.feedback: A run-on has no punctuation at all between the clauses. Here a comma is present.
A fragment lacks a subject or a verb. Both halves here are complete clauses.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which verb is understood but not repeated in the second and third clauses?
hints: Read the first clause, then lend its verb to the second.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Is': each later clause means 'your boasted liberty is an unholy license'. The comma marks where the verb was left out.

questions.onCorrect: “Is” is understood in the later clauses. The comma marks the gap where it was left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a subject or a complement, not a verb. Find the verb the first clause lends to the others.
The missing verb is borrowed from the first clause exactly as it stands there.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
hints: Test the words before each colon: could they stand as a sentence?

acceptedIdeas: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A colon needs a complete clause before it, and what follows should explain or specify. Only the first sentence meets both conditions.

choices.label: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
The motion: failed by two votes.
The reasons were: cost and delay.

questions.onCorrect: A colon needs a full clause before it, and what follows should explain it. Only this sentence meets both.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the words before the colon: “The motion” cannot stand as a sentence.
“The reasons were” cannot stand as a sentence, so a colon after it is misplaced.

questions.prompt: Repair 'It was late, we left' by keeping the comma and adding a coordinating conjunction that states cause and result. Which conjunction do you add?
hints: The second clause is the result of the first. Which short word introduces a result?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'So': 'It was late, so we left.' 'And' would join the clauses without naming the cause.

questions.onCorrect: “So” names the result. “It was late, so we left” says why they left, which “and” would not.

misconceptions.feedback: “And” only adds a second fact. Ask how the second clause relates to the first.
“But” signals contrast. Here the second clause follows from the first.
“Because” opens a dependent clause and would not follow a comma here. Use a coordinating conjunction.

questions.prompt: Douglass writes 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' Keeping the comma, which coordinating conjunction would make this standard edited prose while keeping the contrast?
hints: Choose the conjunction that sets one clause against the other.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'But' or 'yet': 'You may rejoice, but I must mourn.' Both name the contrast; 'and' would flatten it.

questions.onCorrect: “But” sets one clause against the other. “Yet” does the same job.

misconceptions.feedback: “And” would flatten the contrast into a plain addition.
“So” gives a result, and rejoicing does not cause mourning.

questions.prompt: How many independent clauses are in 'The hall was full; the speaker was late: his train had stopped outside the city.'?
hints: Find each subject with its finite verb.
Check whether any clause opens with a subordinator such as 'because' or 'when'.
Each mark here separates complete clauses.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'The hall was full', 'the speaker was late' and 'his train had stopped outside the city'. The colon introduces the reason for the lateness.

questions.onCorrect: Three: each of the three clauses has its own subject and verb, and the marks separate them.

misconceptions.feedback: Two is close. Check the part after the colon: it is a full clause too.
Each mark here separates complete clauses, so there is more than one.
Count only subject-and-verb pairs, and check that each could stand as a sentence.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'The motion was rejected by the committee' in the active voice. How many words does the active sentence have?
hints: Make the actor, the committee, the subject.
Use the past-tense verb without 'was', and drop 'by'.
Count every word, including both articles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 'The committee rejected the motion.' The passive took seven.

questions.onCorrect: Five words: “The committee rejected the motion.” The actor leads and the passive's extra words go.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Rewrite it with the committee acting, then count.
Drop both “was” and “by”: the participle becomes a plain past verb.
You have lost a word. Count both articles.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'Mistakes were made by the finance office' in the active voice. What becomes the subject?
hints: Find the 'by' phrase: whoever sits inside it performed the action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The finance office made mistakes.' The actor, hidden in the 'by' phrase, moves into the subject position.

questions.onCorrect: The finance office made mistakes. The actor, hidden in the “by” phrase, moves into the subject.

misconceptions.feedback: “Mistakes” is the receiver. In the active sentence it follows the verb.

questions.prompt: Unbury the verbs in 'The committee made a decision to conduct a review of the policy': 'made a decision' becomes 'decided' and 'conduct a review of' becomes 'review'. How many words does the revision save?
hints: Count the words in the original sentence.
Write out the revision and count it.
Subtract the revised count from the original count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twelve words become seven: 'The committee decided to review the policy.' Five are saved.

questions.onCorrect: Twelve words become seven, so the revision saves five. Buried verbs cost words and force.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original length. The question asks how many words the revision saves.
That is the length of the revision. Subtract it from the original.
Recount each sentence one word at a time, then check the subtraction.

questions.prompt: Cut the empty frame 'In my opinion, it is true that' and the redundant words 'personal', 'basically' and 'final' from 'In my personal opinion, it is basically true that the final outcome depends on the weather.' How many words remain?
hints: Count the original sentence first.
Count the frame words and the redundant words you are removing.
Subtract, then check by reading what is left aloud.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sixteen words lose ten: 'The outcome depends on the weather.' Six remain.

questions.onCorrect: Six words remain: sixteen lose ten. Cutting padding keeps the claim and loses only noise.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the words you cut. Count what is left.
That is the original length. Remove the frame and the repeated words first.
Check that you removed every word listed, including the three modifiers.

questions.prompt: 'The budget was approved by the council in March.' How many words does the active version save?
hints: Put the council in the subject position.
Write the active sentence and count it.
Subtract the active count from the passive count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine words become seven: 'The council approved the budget in March.' Two are saved.

questions.onCorrect: Nine words become seven, so two are saved. Moving the actor forward drops “was” and “by”.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the passive's own length. Count the active version and subtract.
That is the active sentence's length. The question asks how many words are saved.

questions.prompt: 'An investigation of the causes was carried out by the board.' Which verb is buried inside the noun 'investigation'?
hints: Remove the noun ending '-ation' and rebuild the verb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Investigate': 'The board investigated the causes' turns the noun back into a verb and the board into the subject.

questions.onCorrect: “Investigation” hides the verb “investigate”. Turn it back and the board becomes the actor.

misconceptions.feedback: “Carried out” is the weak verb propping the noun up. Look inside the noun itself.

questions.prompt: Three statements: 'Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.' 'The bridge should close to lorries.' 'A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.' Which is the claim?
hints: Ask which statement the others are reasons for.

acceptedIdeas: The bridge should close to lorries.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The bridge should close to lorries' is the conclusion the other two statements are offered to support.

choices.label: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.

questions.onCorrect: The bridge should close to lorries: the other two statements are offered as its reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a fact offered in support. Ask which statement the others are reasons for.
That is a general rule linking fact to conclusion, so it supports something else.

questions.prompt: Grounds: 'The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.' Claim: 'The defendant handled the knife.' What is Toulmin's name for the unstated rule 'Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it'?
hints: The element authorises the step from evidence to conclusion; the same word names a document that authorises a search.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The warrant: the general principle that authorises the move from these grounds to this claim.

questions.onCorrect: The warrant is the general principle that authorises the move from these grounds to this claim.

misconceptions.feedback: The claim is the conclusion, here the statement about handling. Name the rule that links the fact to it.
The grounds are the fingerprints themselves. The question asks for the rule behind the step.
Backing supports that rule. The question asks for the rule itself.

questions.prompt: In 'Harriet will probably win, unless rain keeps her supporters at home', which single word is the qualifier?
hints: Find the word that measures how confident the claim is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Probably' limits the force of the claim; 'unless rain keeps her supporters at home' is the rebuttal, the condition under which it fails.

questions.onCorrect: “Probably” limits the force of the claim. The “unless” clause is the rebuttal.

misconceptions.feedback: That part names what could go wrong. Find the word that measures how sure the writer is.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise. (2) Customers buy less of a product when its price rises. (3) The price should return to its old level. (4) Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen. Give the number of the statement that is the warrant.
hints: Find the claim first: the statement the others support.
Find the observed fact; that is the grounds.
The warrant is a general rule rather than a particular fact.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 is the warrant: a general rule linking the sales figure (grounds, statement 1) to the pricing claim (statement 3). Statement 4 is the rebuttal.

questions.onCorrect: Statement 2 is the warrant: a general rule linking the sales figure to the pricing claim.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a particular observed fact, so it supplies the grounds.
That is what the writer wants accepted: the claim.
That names exceptions that would limit the argument, so it is a rebuttal.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) The museum should open late every Thursday. (2) Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late. (3) A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost. (4) The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last. Give the number of the statement that supplies the grounds.
hints: Find the statement the others support.
Grounds are particular observed facts, not general rules.
The last statement limits the argument rather than supporting it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 supplies the grounds: an observed fact. Statement 1 is the claim, 3 the warrant and 4 a rebuttal.

questions.onCorrect: Statement 2 is an observed fact, so it supplies the grounds for the claim in statement 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the others support, so it is the claim.
That is a general rule, not an observed fact.
That limits the argument. It does not support it.

questions.prompt: A writer supports the warrant 'Damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads' by citing the national bridge inspection code. In Toulmin's model, what is that support called?
hints: The support is aimed at the rule, not at the conclusion.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Backing: support for the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

questions.onCorrect: Backing supports the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: Grounds support the claim. This support is aimed at the rule behind it.
A qualifier limits how strongly the claim is made. It supports nothing.

questions.prompt: Douglass tells his Rochester audience, “This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.” His right to say it rests on his own life as a man who had escaped slavery. Which of Aristotle's appeals works through the speaker's character and standing?
hints: The Greek word is the root of 'ethics'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: the persuasive force of the speaker's character and credibility.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos: Douglass's own life as a man who had escaped slavery gives him the standing to say it.

misconceptions.feedback: Pathos works on the audience's feelings. Here the force comes from who is speaking.
Logos is the argument itself. Ask what gives Douglass the right to say these words.
Kairos is about timing. Ask what the speaker's own life lends to the claim.

questions.prompt: 'The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.' The image of 'stripes and death' is aimed chiefly at the audience's feelings. Which appeal is this?
hints: The Greek root also gives English 'sympathy'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: the appeal to the audience's emotions, here pity and shame.

questions.onCorrect: Pathos: “stripes and death” is chosen to move the hearers, and it makes the contrast physical.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos is about the speaker's standing. This image is aimed at the hearers' feelings.
Nothing here is reasoned from premise to consequence. The image is chosen to move the audience.

questions.prompt: Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg in November 1863. 'Four score and seven years ago' points back to which year?
hints: A score is twenty.
Four score and seven is four twenties plus seven.
Subtract that number of years from the year of the speech.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

questions.onCorrect: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 takes the nation back to the Declaration.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the year of the speech. Subtract the years the phrase names.
That is how many years, not the year the phrase points back to.
That is the Constitution's year. Work out four twenties plus seven and take it from the year of the speech.

questions.prompt: Douglass delivered his attack on slavery at a celebration of American independence, the day after the Fourth of July. Which Greek term names a speaker's use of the right moment and occasion?
hints: It is the term often added to Aristotle's three appeals, and it means the opportune moment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Kairos: the timeliness of a speech, the fit between argument and occasion.

questions.onCorrect: Kairos: the fit between a speech and the moment it is spoken in.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are Aristotle's three proofs. The question asks for the term about timing.

questions.prompt: Lincoln says the war is 'testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.' He reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake. Which appeal is this chiefly?
hints: Look for the appeal named after the Greek for 'word' or 'reason'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Logos: an appeal through reasoning from premise to consequence.

questions.onCorrect: Logos: Lincoln reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos concerns the speaker's character. This sentence reasons from a premise to a consequence.
The sentence moves from premise to consequence rather than stirring feeling.

questions.prompt: A charity letter opens: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years, I have seen what a missed vaccination can do.' Which appeal does the opening clause make first?
hints: Look at what the opening clause tells you about the writer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years' establishes the writer's experience and credibility before anything else.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos: “As a children's nurse for twenty years” establishes experience and credibility first.

misconceptions.feedback: No emotional image has appeared yet. Look at what the opening clause says about the writer.
Nothing in the opening clause is about the moment or the occasion.

questions.prompt: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness.' How many times does 'it was' open a clause in this extract?
hints: Split the extract at each comma.
Mark the first two words of each clause.
Count the clauses that open the same way.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four. The repeated opening is anaphora; in the full sentence Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses.

questions.onCorrect: Four. The repeated opening is anaphora, and Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses in the full sentence.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how long the full sentence keeps the frame going. Count only the extract shown.
Look again: one more clause opens the same way.
Mark the first two words of every clause, not just the first pair.
Count only the clauses that open with the repeated words.

questions.prompt: Lincoln sets 'what we say here' against 'what they did here' in matching grammatical form. Name the figure that balances opposed ideas in parallel structure.
hints: The Greek name means 'setting against'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Antithesis: contrasting ideas placed in parallel form, here saying against doing and 'we' against 'they'.

questions.onCorrect: Antithesis: opposed ideas, saying against doing and “we” against “they”, in matching grammatical form.

misconceptions.feedback: Chiasmus reverses the order of terms. Here the frame stays the same and the words oppose.
Anaphora is repetition at the start of clauses. The point here is the opposition inside a matching frame.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.' The terms return in reverse order, A B B A. Name the figure.
hints: The name comes from the Greek letter chi, shaped like an X.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus (strictly antimetabole, since the same words return): A B, then B A.

questions.onCorrect: Chiasmus (strictly antimetabole, since the same words return): A B, then B A.

misconceptions.feedback: The ideas do oppose, but what defines this figure is that the order of terms reverses.
Nothing repeats at the start of clauses. Look at the order of the terms in each half.

questions.prompt: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people.' Name the figure made of three parallel members.
hints: The Greek prefix for three is joined to the word for a clause or limb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three prepositional phrases sharing one noun.

questions.onCorrect: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three prepositional phrases sharing one noun.

misconceptions.feedback: Anaphora repeats an opening word. The question asks about the three-part pattern itself.
Nothing is set against anything here. Count the parallel members.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which figure does the repeated opening 'your' create?
hints: Repetition at the start of successive clauses has a name from the Greek for 'carrying back'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Anaphora: repetition at the start of successive clauses, here pointing each charge at the audience.

questions.onCorrect: Anaphora: repetition at the start of successive clauses, here pointing each charge at the audience.

misconceptions.feedback: The series does run to three, but the figure the repeated opening creates is a different one.
The charges are not set against opposites. Look at how each clause begins.

questions.prompt: The witches in Macbeth chant 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair.' Which figure is this?
hints: Look at the order of the two repeated words in each half.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus: fair, foul / foul, fair. The reversal suits a play in which appearances invert.

questions.onCorrect: Chiasmus: fair, foul, then foul, fair. The reversal suits a play in which appearances invert.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing repeats at the start of clauses here. Check the order of the two words in each half.
There is no series of three members. Look at how the two repeated words are ordered.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'
hints: Say the line slowly and tap once for each vowel sound.
'Compare' and 'summer's' have two syllables each.
Every other word has one syllable; add them up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten: shall / I / com / pare / thee / to / a / sum / mer's / day.

questions.onCorrect: Ten: shall, I, com, pare, thee, to, a, sum, mer's, day. Each beat sits on every second syllable.

misconceptions.feedback: “Summer's” has two syllables, not three. Tap once for each vowel sound.
“Compare” and “summer's” have two syllables each, so a syllable is missing from your count.
That is the number of words. Count syllables instead.

questions.prompt: In a regular line of iambic pentameter the beats fall on the even-numbered syllables. Counting from the first syllable, on which syllable does the third beat fall?
hints: List the syllable positions that carry beats.
The first beat falls on the second syllable.
Each further beat comes two syllables later.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Syllable 6: the beats fall on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.

questions.onCorrect: Syllable 6: the beats fall on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the beat's number. The question asks which syllable it falls on, counting from the start of the line.
The first beat is on the second syllable. Step on two syllables at a time.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in 'That looks on tempests and is never shaken'?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Tempests', 'never' and 'shaken' have two syllables each.
Notice what follows the last beat on 'sha-'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Eleven. '-ken' is an extra unstressed syllable after the last beat on 'sha-': a feminine ending.

questions.onCorrect: Eleven: “-ken” is an extra unstressed syllable after the last beat, a feminine ending.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for a regular line. This one has an extra syllable at the end.
“Tempests”, “never” and “shaken” have two syllables each. Recount.

questions.prompt: The witches chant 'Double, double, toil and trouble': DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble. Each foot falls from stressed to unstressed. Name this foot.
hints: Its Greek name means 'running'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The trochee: stressed then unstressed, the reverse of the iamb. Four trochees make trochaic tetrameter.

questions.onCorrect: The trochee: stressed then unstressed, the reverse of the iamb.

misconceptions.feedback: An iamb rises, weak then strong. The witches' foot does the opposite.
A dactyl has three syllables. These feet have two.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in Dickinson's 'That perches in the soul'?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Perches' has two syllables.
Count the remaining one-syllable words and add them.
